card.thesis: In liquid, heavily-owned AI/semiconductor-cycle names, a short, sharp price dislocation -- a 2-3 session air-pocket severe enough to push RSI(3) under 15 while price pierces a tight 10-day Bollinger band -- is usually forced-flow selling (stop cascades, options-dealer delta hedging, single-headline overreaction) rather than a genuine repricing of the business, and forced flow exhausts itself in days, not weeks. On this universe over 2021-02-13 through 2026-02-13, 306 such dislocations resolved (price closing back above ema(5)) in a median of 4 sessions and a mean of 4.4, with only 4.2% still unresolved after 10 sessions -- so the reversion this trades is fast almost every time it happens at all, which is exactly the profile a tight max_hold_days is built for. The other side of this trade is whoever sold into the panic at the worst print: momentum/CTA systematic sellers extending a move 1-3 sessions past where fundamentals justify, and retail stop-outs clearing into thin liquidity. Exiting on the first close back above ema(5) -- not waiting for a full return to the 10- or 20-day mean -- is deliberate: in the same sample the median bounce at that first ema(5) reclaim was +2.8% (mean +2.7%), most of which happens in the first 3-4 sessions, so waiting longer trades a small amount of extra upside for a large amount of extra exposure to the move failing. This is a high win-rate, small-average-win system by design, which is precisely the profile a single oversized loss can erase, so the stop is sized deliberately wider than the typical adverse move (median intra-hold drawdown was -3.6%, so a 7% stop is roughly twice the typical noise) rather than tight to the entry, and a 5% take-profit locks in the strong minority of bounces before they have a chance to round-trip.
card.entry: rsi(3) < 15 and close < bb_lower(10,2)

card.thesis: Method: across all 14 catalog managers' filings public by 2026-02-13 (as_of filters on filing date, never period), I counted how many independently hold each of the 43 tradeable roster tickers, mapping CUSIP to ticker via the repo's own ledger bridge. Two managers were excluded from that count before anything else: RENTECH (3,185 total positions) and BRIDGEWATER (1,040) individually cover 51% and 63% of the entire 43-name roster -- a name appearing in either book is barely more informative than a coin flip, because these two own almost everything liquid. The remaining 12 'selective' managers cover a mean of 15.3% of the roster each (range 0%-33%, BRK/PERSHING/SCION/ELLIOTT near zero, ARKINVEST/COATUE near a third), which is a plausible base rate for actual selection rather than near-universal coverage, so I built the crowding score from those 12 only. Mapping loss, reported as instructed: 5,071 raw holdings across all 14 managers, 220 (4.3%) resolved to any ticker via CUSIP, and 4,851 (95.7%) did not -- expected, per the addendum, because the bridge only knows CUSIPs the user has personally traded, not a general CUSIP directory. Of the 220 mapped rows, 128 fall on the 43-symbol roster. That means this whole exercise runs on a narrow, ledger-biased slice: 'crowded' here means 'held by several selective managers AND already something the user has owned or watched,' not 'crowded across the market.' Staleness, exactly as the addendum's table states: 10 of the 12 selective managers (BRK, PERSHING, SCION, APPALOOSA, DUQUESNE, THIRDPOINT, ELLIOTT, TIGERGLOBAL, COATUE, LONEPINE) show Q3-2025 positions, 140 days stale at trade start (2026-02-17); ARKINVEST and SOROS show Q4-2025, 48 days stale. Sign test, as instructed: I computed trailing 3-month, 6-month and 1-year returns through the design cutoff for the 24 roster tickers that any selective manager held (crowding score 1-10), and correlated (Spearman, rank-based, robust to the one extreme outlier SNDK, a +1,242% 6-month move) against the crowding score. Results: 3m rho=+0.24 (all 24) / +0.36 (excl. SNDK); 6m rho=+0.17 / +0.27; 1y rho=+0.25 (n=23). All positive, none large, and the critical value for significance at n~23 (two-sided, alpha=0.05) is about 0.41 -- not one of these clears it, with or without the outlier. A high-crowd (score>=5, n=6: AMZN TSM META MSFT GOOGL NVDA) vs low-crowd (score<=2, n=12-13) bucket split tells an inconsistent story across windows: high beat low on 3m (-1.2% vs -8.2% all-24, -1.2% vs -19.0% ex-SNDK) but roughly matched or lagged on 6m and 1y once the SNDK outlier moves out of the low bucket. That is 'neither, convincingly' -- 14 managers filtered down to 11-24 overlapping names is nowhere near enough independent information to separate 'many good investors converged for a reason' from 'a crowded trade has no marginal buyer left,' and I am not going to assert a direction the data does not support. What I did about it: I do not use crowding to rank, size, or time entries -- I use it only as the addendum requires, as a universe filter, and treat the sign question as unresolved rather than pick one to sound decisive. The investable universe is every ticker with a crowding score >=3 (at least 3 of the 12 selective, independent processes hold it): AMD AMZN AVGO GOOGL META MSFT NFLX NVDA TSLA TSM UNH -- 11 names, dropping the crowd-1/2 tickers (idiosyncratic single- or double-manager bets, no more informative than an arbitrary stock pick) and the giants' contribution. Timing is carried entirely by price, per the addendum's own constraint that the DSL has no 13F terms: enter on a confirmed uptrend that is not already extended (close above both its 50- and 150-day averages, RSI(14) under 70, so the entry lags a fresh breakout rather than chasing one), exit on trend break or momentum fade (close below its 50-day average, or RSI(14) under 40). Mechanism, for whichever story turns out true: if this is validation, buying only names multiple independent, well-resourced processes already own, and only once price itself confirms the trend, should see fewer false starts than an unfiltered momentum screen; if it is fragility, the same filter is buying into names with the least room for a new buyer, and the trend-break exit is the only defence available, on the same delayed, close-based trigger every card in this tournament has to accept. On the other side of every entry: momentum traders already positioned before the RSI/sma filter confirms, and anyone who sold into a crowded name expecting exactly the fragility story to play out. Two engine limits I am not working around: this is a single frozen snapshot for the whole six-month window -- a real 13F strategy would refresh at the Q4-2025 stragglers (~2026-02-17) and Q1-2026 filings (~2026-05-15), both inside the trading window, and this engine cannot rotate a universe mid-run, so treat this as one stale six-month bet, not a live 13F strategy. And stop_loss_pct/position_pct are single fixed numbers: ATR(14)/close across these 11 names at 2026-02-13 ranges from 3.3% (NFLX) to 7.1% (AMD), mean 4.4%, so the 10% stop below is roughly 2.3x the average name's daily range but only ~1.4x AMD's -- AMD and TSLA (ann. vol 62-64%) are the volatility-mismatched names in an otherwise 26-51% ann.-vol universe, and I am keeping them in rather than quietly dropping the two names crowding independently flagged.
card.entry: close > sma(50) and close > sma(150) and rsi(14) < 70

card.thesis: Round 1 established that fresh 13F initiations are a weak signal even where the mapping works: 934 NEW disclosures across fourteen managers through as_of=2026-02-13, 22 tradeable, 912 lost to unmapped CUSIPs, and a 52% beat-benchmark rate among the ones that did map -- a coin flip whose mean was carried by two outliers. Round 2 asks whether that signal reaches this 93-symbol roster at all, and the honest answer is no. First, the empirical check the brief asked for: the CUSIP-to-ticker bridge is the user's own ledger (app.institutions.catalog.ledger_cusip_tickers), so I read every (cusip, primary_symbol) pair the ledger actually holds -- 119 rows, 119 unique tickers -- and intersected that set against the round-2 roster's 93 symbols. Six overlap: GDX, GDXJ, IGV, SLV, TLT, XBI. Not zero, which the brief said was a live empirical question rather than something to assume either way -- but not enough to build on, for a reason that shows up the moment you check what the fourteen managers actually hold. Querying load_latest(as_of=2026-02-13) for all fourteen catalog managers, only two hold any of those six tickers at all: BRIDGEWATER (IGV, weight 0.109% of a 1040-line book) and RENTECH (XBI 0.008%, GDX 0.006%, IGV 0.005% of a 3185-line book). The other twelve -- BRK, ARKINVEST, PERSHING, SCION, APPALOOSA, DUQUESNE, SOROS, THIRDPOINT, ELLIOTT, TIGERGLOBAL, COATUE, LONEPINE -- hold zero. Narrowing to what a momentum-on-fresh-initiations strategy actually needs, NEW rows specifically: across all 934 NEW disclosures in the most recent public delta for every manager (identical universe of filings to round 1's count, since as_of is unchanged), exactly 2 map to a round-2 roster ticker -- Bridgewater's IGV (new, 281,938 shares, 0.109% weight) and Rentech's XBI (new, 0.008% weight). Both are from the two books round 1's own thesis explicitly excluded as not comparable to a concentrated manager's conviction buy ("a NEW row there is a 0.01-0.5% sliver of an index-like or systematic book, not a decision") -- applying that same standard here rather than relaxing it because the sample got smaller, zero of the ten concentrated, genuinely stock-picking managers I would have trusted as a signal in round 1 have a single fresh initiation that reaches this roster. The ledger cannot name JNJ or XLU or TLT, as the brief predicted, and the two names it can name arrive at 0.005%-0.109% weight inside billion-line systematic macro books -- portfolio arithmetic, not a decision. Total holdings mapping loss across all fourteen managers' latest snapshots: 5071 holdings, 4 mapped to a round-2 roster ticker (0.08%), all four from the two excluded books. I looked for the mapping rather than assuming it away and found it is real but unusable -- this is the 'no, and here is what I did about it' the brief asked for. So this card carries no 13F signal at all; the discipline is still momentum, expressed as pure price-trend confirmation, standing on its own per the brief's explicit instruction. Mechanism: names the market has already started to trend tend to keep trending over multi-month horizons -- underreaction to slowly-diffusing information (analyst estimates and institutional flows adjust in stages, not on the print) and trend-following capital that arrives after a move is already underway, both documented cross-asset (Jegadeesh-Titman 1993 for single-name momentum, Moskowitz-Ooi-Pedersen 2012 for time-series momentum across equities, bonds and commodities). The other side of the trade: value-discipline holders capping exposure into strength and short sellers fading a name that 'already ran,' both selling into a trend that has further to go before the market has fully re-rated it. I measured trailing-252-session return, 126-session (6-month) and 63-session (3-month) return, annualized volatility, and pct-of-days-above-sma(200) for all 93 round-2 symbols through 2026-02-13. Metals/thematic names (SLV +102% 126d, GDXJ +87%, GDX +80%, PPLT +51%) showed the strongest momentum by far but at 43-56% annualized volatility -- a single fixed stop_loss_pct cannot fit both that and a calmer name, per this brief's own engine-constraint warning, so I did not build on them; a metals-only card would be a legitimate but different strategy than the one asked for here. Instead I selected eight names in a comparable volatility band (19.1%-33.2% annualized, a 14-point spread versus the roster's full range of near-zero to 56%) that were simultaneously trending -- close above both sma(50) and sma(200) as of the cutoff, and 40%-99% of the trailing year spent above sma(200) -- and that measured genuinely diversified against each other: mean pairwise correlation 0.253 over the trailing 259 sessions (min 0.026, max 0.568), well under the 0.581 this brief measured for the round-2 sector-ETF cluster and the 0.589 round-1 measured for its semiconductor cluster. Universe, ordered by measured 126-session return (the tiebreak the brief flagged): CAT (industrials, +85.4%, 33.2% vol), JNJ (healthcare, +39.3%, 19.1% vol -- the exact name this brief said the ledger could not resolve, reached here on price alone, no 13F claim attached), XOM (energy, +38.3%, 24.8% vol), XBI (biotech, +37.2%, 27.9% vol), EWZ (Brazil equity, +36.5%, 25.0% vol), ICLN (clean energy, +34.9%, 24.4% vol), WMT (retail staple, +32.8%, 25.9% vol), NEE (utility, +29.8%, 26.6% vol) -- eight genuinely different sectors and one non-US-equity country fund, not eleven costumes on the same trade. Entry requires close > sma(50) and close > sma(200) and rsi(14) > 50: trend confirmed on two horizons plus a momentum floor, deliberately unoptimized and structurally identical to the trend filter round 1 validated conceptually (there, filtering a 13F-curated list; here, filtering the whole selection). Exit is a trend break (close crosses_below sma(50)), backed by a 10% stop and a 120-day time stop so the position cannot ride a slow bleed indefinitely if the trend-break rule is late to fire. What I did differently from round 1, and why: round 1 used 13F to pick a universe and price rules to time entry. Round 2 could not do that -- the mapping check above shows the 13F leg contributes nothing on this roster -- so the universe selection itself is now driven by the same measured momentum/trend/diversification criteria that round 1 only applied inside the entry rule. This is not a refusal to use the new freedom the round-2 roster offers; it is a direct consequence of checking the constraint the brief asked me to check, finding it binding, and building the strategy the discipline can actually support instead of forcing a thin 13F narrative onto two 0.01%-weight portfolio-management rows in billion-line macro books. What I expect to go wrong: momentum strategies crash together in a correlated risk-off shock -- CAT, XOM, EWZ and ICLN all carry real cyclical/growth-factor exposure that measured low pairwise correlation in a trending 2024-2026 regime but has historically converged toward 1 in a broad selloff (2022, 2020-Q1), which the 259-session correlation window used here cannot see because it barely includes such an episode. XBI and ICLN are the most volatile names in the set and have the fastest, sharpest mean-reversion crashes in this roster's history when a multi-month run ends -- a stop evaluated on the previous close, not the intraday low, will be late and expensive exactly when that happens. EWZ carries country-specific political and currency risk with no relationship to US price trend at all. And the entry rule is the same simple trend-and-momentum filter this discipline always uses: it will underperform, possibly badly, in a choppy, range-bound regime with no sustained trend in any of these eight names, which six months is not enough time to rule out.
card.entry: close > sma(50) and close > sma(200) and rsi(14) > 50

card.thesis: This card is organised around the payoff shape, not the signal: a deliberately low win rate traded for a large reward-to-risk, so the edge lives in the few trades that become real trend continuations, not in being right often. The universe is ten early-stage AI-infrastructure/power/compute names (memory, networking optics, neocloud capacity, nuclear/fuel, crypto infra) whose re-ratings are lumpy rather than smooth: most sessions are noise around a range, but a real catalyst -- a capacity contract, a beat that resets estimates, a sector-wide re-rating -- can add 25-40%+ over a few weeks as sell-side models and momentum/CTA flow catch up with news that was already public. The entry (close > bb_upper(20,2) and macd_hist(12,26,9) > 0 and close > sma(50)) tries to catch that catalyst near its start -- a statistically unusual band breakout, confirmed by accelerating momentum, inside an already-established uptrend -- rather than after the move has already priced. The other side of the initial breakout bar is whoever fades the 'overbought' print or takes first-day profit; both are wrong on average during the minority of breakouts that actually extend, which is exactly the tail this card is priced to capture and the majority that don't is exactly the cost of admission. Measured through 2026-02-13 on this ten-symbol cohort, trailing ATR(14)/price runs 6.3% (MU) to 14.0% (IREN) and the 90th-percentile absolute daily close-to-close move runs roughly 5%-12%, well above the <2% level a tight stop would need for SGOV or GLD -- stop_loss_pct and position_pct are single fixed numbers with no per-symbol scaling, so I built a universe narrow enough that one stop is a defensible approximation and left out both the cash-like names and the very calmest large-caps in the 43-symbol list. I set stop_loss_pct=0.08: above the p90 single-day move for seven of the ten names (so an ordinary bad session confirmed on the next close does not itself trigger it), but I confirmed it does sit inside normal noise for IREN, OKLO and APLD specifically (their own p90 daily moves run 10.6%-12.4%), and expect those three to be stopped out by ordinary chop more often than the rest of the book -- a mismatch I am accepting, not hiding. Simulating this exact entry against an 8% stop, 28% target and a 90-trading-day time stop over each symbol's full available history (496 qualifying, de-duplicated signals, min. 10 sessions apart): the target was reached before the stop 35.3% of the time (weighted), the stop was hit first 57.3% of the time, and only 7.5% of trades ran out the 90-day clock unresolved; measured independently of the stop, a 28%+ high was reached at some point within 90 sessions on 37.7% of signals, confirming these names do produce moves of this size often enough to be worth pricing for, not just occasionally. Median max adverse excursion across all signals was -8% to -9%, almost exactly the stop level -- ordinary pullbacks bottom close to where the stop sits, not far beyond it, which is the check the brief asks for before trusting a tight stop on daily bars. Planned reward:risk is take_profit_pct/stop_loss_pct = 0.28/0.08 = 3.5. I expect the realised ratio to fall well short of that: the 35% target-hit rate above is measured across 10-40+ years of history per name, but the trading window is a single 127-session draw, so the realistic trade count for any one name in that window is small (roughly 1-3 signals each in the design-window base rate), meaning a handful of trades will decide the whole result and the 7.5% timeout rate measured in the long sample could easily be the dominant outcome in six months if no name's breakout resolves cleanly either way before the time stop -- in which case the realised reward:risk will track the average timeout return, not 3.5, and the report's side-by-side comparison should be read with that in mind rather than as a broken plan. With a 57% base stop-first rate, expect long stretches of small losses between winners: the low win rate is not a flaw to explain away but the entire point of the payoff shape, and it means this card needs 10-20+ resolved trades before its win rate is more than noise. Position sizing (max_positions=6, position_pct=0.12, 72% max deployed) is deliberately smaller per name than a trend-following card would use, because the majority-loser payoff shape only works if no single 8% stop-out is large enough to matter, while still keeping six of ten names live so the book has enough simultaneous shots at the rare 28%+ winner.
card.entry: close > bb_upper(20,2) and macd_hist(12,26,9) > 0 and close > sma(50)

card.thesis: The angle is conviction weight: a manager's largest position by portfolio share is the one they were most willing to be publicly wrong about, and that only means something in a book small enough that a top position is a real bet rather than a rounding error -- which is why RENTECH (3,185 positions) and BRIDGEWATER (1,040) are excluded on their face and never queried. Universe was built from the two concentrated 13F managers whose disclosed holdings, as of the 2026-02-13 design cutoff, actually mapped to tradeable roster tickers with meaningful weight: PERSHING (period 2025-09-30, filed 2025-11-14, 11 positions -- Bill Ackman) and APPALOOSA (period 2025-09-30, filed 2025-11-13, 45 positions -- David Tepper). A holding qualifies only if its weight-within-that-manager's-book exceeds an equal-weight bar (1/11 for Pershing, 1/45 for Appaloosa) -- an objective 'this is actually overweighted' test, not a top-K pick. That leaves 8 names: AMZN and GOOGL from Pershing (2 of 11 raw positions mapped -- 9 lost, mostly UBER, BROOKFIELD, HOWARD HUGHES, RESTAURANT BRANDS, and a separate GOOG Class-C line the roster does not carry); AMZN, NVDA, TSM, META, MSFT, QCOM and AMD from Appaloosa (9 of 45 raw positions mapped -- 36 lost; MU and UNH also mapped but fell below Appaloosa's own 2.2% average-weight bar and were cut by the same rule that let the other seven in). Three other manager books were checked and contributed nothing. SCION (period 2025-09-30, filed 2025-11-03, 8 positions -- Michael Burry) mapped zero tradeable tickers, and more importantly its top four holdings by weight -- Palantir 66%, Nvidia 13.5%, Pfizer 11.1%, Halliburton 4.5%, together 95% of the disclosed book -- are PUT and CALL option lines, not equity shares; treating a Burry 13F 'top holding' as a bullish conviction pick would have been backwards, since the largest position was a bet against Palantir, not for it. ELLIOTT (period 2025-09-30, filed 2025-11-14, 35 positions -- Paul Singer) also mapped zero: only one line (EQIX) resolved a ticker at all and EQIX is not on the roster, and roughly 28% of the disclosed book by weight is itself index/sector-ETF puts and calls (QQQ, sector SPDRs, iShares) -- a hedge book, not a stock-picker's conviction list. BRK (period 2025-09-30, filed 2025-11-14, 41 positions -- Warren Buffett) mapped 3 tickers (GOOGL, AMZN, UNH) but all three sit below Berkshire's own 2.4% average-weight bar, so the same objective filter that built the rest of the universe excludes Berkshire entirely; its real largest position, Apple at 22.7% of the book, is not on the 43-symbol roster at all. At TRADE_START (2026-02-17) the surviving data is 95-96 days stale from filing and describes positions as they stood 140 days earlier; because this engine cannot rotate a universe mid-run, that snapshot is what the strategy trades for the full six-month window, aging to roughly nine months stale by 2026-08-18 with no way to see whether either manager has since exited. I tested whether the premise is even true in the one window I am allowed to look at: from 2025-11-14 (the latest of the two managers' filing dates -- the first day this information was actually public) through the 2026-02-13 cutoff, the equal-weighted 8-name conviction basket returned -3.93%, versus +10.13% for the equal-weighted 43-symbol trading roster and -1.13% for QQQM, a closer like-for-like large-cap-growth benchmark. Only 3 of 8 names (GOOGL +10.6%, TSM +28.6%, META +5.0%) beat QQQM over that window; AMZN, NVDA, MSFT, QCOM and AMD all lagged it, three of them (MSFT -21.3%, QCOM -19.1%, AMD -16.0%) by double digits. Over the only window I can check, buying what these managers were conviction-weighted into performed worse than an index benchmark and worse than doing nothing special -- that is folklore, not edge, and I am not building a buy-and-hold card on it. Instead the 13F data does exactly one job here: it picks the 8-name universe. Whether and when to actually own each name is decided by price alone, gated to require that the market has already been agreeing with the position over both an intermediate (50-day) and long (200-day) horizon, with RSI capped under 70 so entries are not chased into names already extended and already selling off the way MSFT, QCOM and AMD were doing for most of the measured window. That is the point of a risk-managed discipline applied to a signal I just measured as unreliable on its own: use it as a candidate list, not a buy trigger, and let price do the confirming. Sizing deliberately does not commit the whole book -- max_positions=6 of the 8 candidates at position_pct=0.15 (90% max exposure, a 10% cash buffer) -- because a risk-managed strategy built on a signal already shown to be weak should not also run fully invested. Stop and target are a fixed 8%/16% (2:1 planned reward:risk) with a 90-day max hold, chosen shorter than the full window specifically because the underlying 13F snapshot keeps aging every day the position is held; a trade that has not resolved in 90 days is running increasingly on stale institutional information regardless of what price is doing, so it is closed on a clock rather than held on the strength of a now much-older filing. On volatility: measured ATR(14)/close at the design cutoff clusters tightly for 7 of the 8 names (AMZN 4.2%, GOOGL 3.6%, NVDA 3.8%, TSM 4.6%, META 4.0%, MSFT 3.8%, QCOM 3.6%), so the single 8% stop sits at roughly 1.7-2.2x ATR for those seven -- a reasonable, not noise-width, distance. AMD is the exception at 7.1% ATR, nearly double the rest of the basket, so the same 8% stop is only about 1.1x AMD's ATR -- close to noise-width, and AMD is disproportionately likely to be stopped out on ordinary chop rather than a genuine trend break. AMD stays in the universe anyway, because it cleared the same overweight-vs-book-average bar as the other seven and cutting it after seeing its volatility would be tuning the universe to flatter the risk math rather than reporting the mismatch, which the brief asks for directly.
card.entry: close > sma(200) and close > sma(50) and rsi(14) < 70

card.thesis: Same engine limitation as round 1: entry/exit are evaluated per symbol against that symbol's own bars, with no cross-sectional comparison, so this still cannot buy 'the strongest sector' or trade a spread -- there is no relative-strength or pairs logic available at all. What changed is the universe, and I used it deliberately. Round 1 forced 9 semiconductor names that correlated at 0.589 average; before assuming round 2's sector ETFs would fix that, I measured them: the 11 US sector ETFs correlate at 0.581 average pairwise over the trailing 259 sessions through 2026-02-13 -- statistically indistinguishable from round 1's semis. Sector-vs-sector rotation is not the diversification round 2 actually offers; equity-vs-duration and equity-vs-gold are. IEF correlates -0.110 with SPY, TLT +0.090, GLD +0.042 -- genuinely uncorrelated, unlike round 1's universe. I also checked the two pairs the brief named directly and neither survived: HYG correlates 0.824 with SPY (it trades like equity beta with a coupon, not a hedge) and HYG vs IEF is only 0.226, not a clean risk-on/risk-off inverse. International (EEM 0.738, FXI 0.522, EWZ 0.491 vs SPY) also correlates with equities more than the 'uncorrelated Brazilian equities' framing suggests, and EEM/FXI correlate 0.847 with each other, so an EM sleeve would not have added a second independent bet either. What I built: apply one absolute trend-confirmation condition (close above its own 50-day average, RSI(14) between 55 and 80) identically across 7 symbols spanning three genuinely different sleeves -- growth equity (XLK, SPY), defensive equity (XLU, XLP), and duration/gold (IEF, TLT, GLD) -- capped at 3 concurrent positions. I tested whether the cap can express real rotation by asking: on sessions where both SPY and XLK fail the trend condition (90 of 260, i.e. equity beta is not confirmed), does anything else confirm instead? GLD qualifies 74.4% of those sessions, IEF 42.2%, XLP 43.3%, TLT only 26.7%, XLU only 17.8%. That is a real, measured complementary relationship -- gold and the shorter-duration bond ETF tend to be in their own confirmed uptrend precisely when growth equity is not -- and it is the closest thing to genuine rotation this absolute-condition-plus-cap design can produce: not because the rule compares assets to each other, but because uncorrelated assets independently satisfy or fail the same rule at different times, and the position cap is what turns that into a forced choice instead of a redundant tiebreak. Universe order is the fill-priority tiebreak on days when more than 3 qualify at once (39% of sessions had 4 or more of the 7 qualify simultaneously): I ordered XLK, SPY, GLD, IEF, XLU, XLP, TLT deliberately -- XLK and SPY first because they had the highest measured qualification rates (52.7%, 61.9%) and the largest sleeve, i.e. the strongest measured trend persistence in this window; GLD third despite being a 'hedge' in the correlation sense because at 59.6% qualification and 24.9% annualized vol it behaved like a trending risk asset in its own right this year, not a passive ballast; IEF ahead of TLT because IEF's qualification behavior was steadier (35.4% vs 26.2%) and the two are 0.889 correlated so there is little reason to want both when only one slot is at stake; XLU and XLP last among the equity sleeves because their co-qualification with a failed equity signal was the weakest (17.8% and 43.3% respectively) of the candidates I measured. On volatility: this universe's spread is far wider than round 1's -- annualized vol ranges from IEF at 5.6% to XLK at 27.3%, and GLD, at 24.9%, is not the cash-like ballast its reputation suggests in this specific window. A single stop_loss_pct cannot fit both ends: at 8% it is roughly 1.4x IEF's entire trailing 260-day max drawdown (-3.5%), so IEF positions will almost never be stopped out and will instead close on the trend-exit rule or the 120-day time stop; the same 8% is well inside normal noise for XLK and GLD (median absolute 10-day move 2.98% and 2.70%), so it will bind there as an actual risk control. I am sizing for the volatile end and accepting that the stop is nearly inert on the quiet end -- the alternative, a stop wide enough to matter for IEF, would be far too loose to protect XLK or GLD. On the other side of these trades: cross-asset risk-parity and macro funds that rotate into duration and gold ahead of confirmation (this rule is a lagging, close-only confirmation and will always be later than a fund trading on rate expectations or positioning data); trend-following CTAs running the same signal faster or with vol-targeting this fixed-size card cannot replicate; and, on the equity sleeves, dip-buyers who re-enter before a 50-day average reclaim confirms and are already positioned by the time this rule agrees.

card.thesis: Same payoff-shape discipline as round 1 -- a deliberately low win rate traded for a large reward-to-risk, so the edge lives in the minority of trades that become real trend continuations, not in being right often -- but round 2's open universe let me measure the tail directly instead of approximating it with the user's own AI/semis holdings. The round-1 card had to fake a low-vol-friendly cohort out of IREN/OKLO/APLD-adjacent names because that was all the 43-symbol book offered; round 2 lifts that constraint, so I went straight at the roster's actual tail-heavy corner -- GDXJ ARKW ARKG TAN ICLN XBI IBB JETS CPER USO -- rather than reusing round 1's semiconductor breakout idea on whatever names happened to be volatile this time. Using the identical mechanism as round 1 (close > bb_upper(20,2) and macd_hist(12,26,9) > 0 and close > sma(50): a statistically unusual band breakout, confirmed by accelerating momentum, inside an established uptrend) I simulated every de-duplicated signal (>=10 sessions apart) on each of those ten names plus GDX/SMH/SLV as comparisons, walking forward up to 90 sessions against an 8% stop and several target sizes, using each name's full available history through 2026-02-13. The finding that mattered: at round 1's own target/stop (28%/8%, RRR 3.5), this roster is meaningfully thinner. Aggregated across the nine names I kept (785 signals), the target was reached first only 15.0% of the time, the stop first 56.4%, with 28.5% timing out at 90 days -- worse on every axis than round 1's measured 35.3% target-first / 57.3% stop-first / 7.5% timeout on the same mechanism. IBB was the clearest case of the brief's warning: 28%+ moves resolved before the stop on just 2.4% of its 127 signals, i.e. it essentially does not produce this discipline's target size within this holding window; USO (9.4%) and ARKG (7.7%) were nearly as thin, and I dropped all three rather than force them into the card. Rather than keep the 3.5:1 target nothing reaches, I brought it down until the hit rate recovered: at 16% target / 8% stop (RRR 2.0) the same nine-name aggregate reaches target_first=32.1%, stop_first=52.9%, timeout=15.0% -- close to round 1's realised base rate, on a target roughly half the size. Universe (ordered by measured target-first/stop-first ratio at 16%/8%, strongest first): ARKW (59 signals, ratio 1.38, target-first 49.2%), TAN (83, 0.68, 38.6%), SMH (139, 0.63, 30.2%), CPER (75, 0.57, 26.7%), XBI (102, 0.57, 29.4%), SLV (112, 0.56, 32.1%), ICLN (76, 0.54, 27.6%), JETS (54, 0.50, 29.6%), GDXJ (85, 0.46, 30.6%). The mechanism: these are thematic/sector funds and single-commodity trackers whose re-ratings are lumpy, not smooth -- a capacity announcement, an inventory print, a growth-scare reversal, a sector-wide re-rating catches sell-side models and momentum/CTA flow still catching up with news already public. The other side of the breakout bar is whoever fades the 'overbought' print or takes first-day theme-fund profit; both are wrong on average during the minority of breakouts that extend, and that minority is exactly what an RRR of 2.0 is priced to capture. Two things I expect to go wrong. First, the arithmetic is close to the line: a naive breakeven on target-first/stop-first alone needs target-first above stop/(stop+target)=33.3%, and the measured 32.1% sits just under it before the rule exit (close < sma(20)) and 90-day timeout are even considered -- this is a thinner edge than round 1's, not a safely larger one, and it may not clear costs. Second, one name in this book is entering the trading window in an already extreme regime: SLV's trailing 14-day ATR/price measured 13.2% at the design cutoff (it round-tripped roughly $80->$109->$67 in three weeks in late January/February 2026 on a physical-silver-squeeze-then-unwind), more than 1.5x the 8% stop itself -- an ordinary session in that regime, confirmed on the next close, could stop the position out before any trend has a chance to develop. That is the same mismatch I disclosed for IREN/OKLO/APLD in round 1, accepted rather than hidden, because the alternative (dropping SLV) would remove one of the two purely idiosyncratic-catalyst names (SLV, CPER) that are not simply growth-equity beta -- and I'd rather keep the diversification and name the risk. Related regime risk: ARKW/SMH/XBI/ICLN/JETS are all duration- and risk-appetite-sensitive funds that tend to move together in a broad tech/growth drawdown even though they sit in different headline sectors, so max_positions=6 buys fewer independent shots at the tail than the position count implies -- a single macro shock could cluster several stop-outs on the same day rather than spread them. Position sizing (max_positions=6, position_pct=0.12, 72% max deployed) matches round 1's philosophy: small enough per name that no single 8% stop-out dominates the book, while keeping enough names live for the rare 16%+ winner to show up somewhere in the trading window.

card.thesis: A manager opening a brand-new 13F position is a decision, not inertia -- but the filing lag makes that decision old news by the time anyone can act on it, and a naive test of the idea shows why that matters. I diffed consecutive filings (through as_of=2026-02-13) for six concentrated, genuinely stock-picking managers -- BRK (41 positions), APPALOOSA (45), DUQUESNE (65), TIGERGLOBAL (56), COATUE (74), LONEPINE (25) -- plus four more with zero tradeable NEW rows this cycle (PERSHING, SCION, ELLIOTT, THIRDPOINT), and excluded SOROS/BRIDGEWATER/RENTECH/ARKINVEST outright: those books hold 244-3185 positions and a 'NEW' row there is a 0.01-0.5% sliver of an index-like or systematic book, not a decision comparable to BRK's 1.6%-weight GOOGL buy. Across 25 tradeable NEW disclosures from the six concentrated managers over the design window (filed 2025-05 through 2026-02), forward return from the filing date to the design cutoff (or 63 trading days, whichever came first) averaged +12.3% (median +9.9%) against a QQQM benchmark average of +4.3% over the same windows -- but the rate at which a NEW disclosure actually beat QQQM over that window was 52%, a coin flip, driven by a few huge winners (SNDK +146%, INTC +96%) offsetting several outright losers (NFLX -31%, ORCL -35%, SNOW -29%, META -22%, AMD -16%). So 'institutions bought it' is not, by itself, an edge in this sample -- it is a high-dispersion bet on names the market had already started arguing about. The entry rule exists to filter that dispersion rather than assume it away: close > sma(50) and close > sma(200) and rsi(14) > 50 requires the market to have already confirmed the uptrend the filing hints at before capital commits, which would have kept this strategy out of ORCL, NFLX, SNOW and META in the sample above (all broke trend before or shortly after their filing became public) while still catching AVGO, GOOGL and the SNDK/INTC outliers once their charts turned up. The other side of the trade is whoever sells into that confirmed strength -- value-discipline holders unwinding into a re-rate, and shorts fading a name that 'already ran' -- while institutional accumulation that began before the filing quietly continues. Universe: the eight roster names with a tradeable NEW row in each manager's latest filing public by 2026-02-13 -- GOOGL (BRK, weight 1.62%; also DUQUESNE, 0.61%), AMD (APPALOOSA, 2.08%), AMZN (DUQUESNE, 2.36%), META (DUQUESNE, 1.38%), SNDK (DUQUESNE, 0.46%), NFLX (TIGERGLOBAL, 0.75%), SNOW (COATUE, 1.08%), AVGO (LONEPINE, 3.72%) -- all from filings covering the quarter ended 2025-09-30, filed 2025-11-13/14. Staleness, confronted directly: a NEW row absent in the 2025-06-30 filing and present in the 2025-09-30 one could have been bought as early as 2025-07-01, giving a worst-case position age of 231 days (7.6 months) by trade start (2026-02-17), and even the best case -- bought the day before quarter-end -- is 140 days old. The manager may have already exited; the next filing that would tell us so (Q4 2025, due ~2026-02-14 to mid-March, and Q1 2026 around 2026-05-15) lands inside the trading window this engine cannot see or rotate into, so this is a single stale six-month snapshot, not a live 13F strategy. Mapping cost: across the six managers used, 69 NEW rows were disclosed and only 9 (13%) mapped to a roster ticker (8 unique names, since GOOGL was independently initiated by two managers) -- the rest were CUSIPs with no ticker in the user's ledger, mostly non-roster names, bonds, or foreign issuers a 13F cannot even report. Across all fourteen catalog managers the ratio is starker: 934 NEW rows, 22 tradeable, 912 lost. My honest view: a four-month-old snapshot of someone else's book is weak information at best -- the 52% naive beat-rate says so plainly -- and this card does not claim otherwise. What it claims is narrower: among names sophisticated concentrated managers found worth a fresh position, the ones the market has already started to confirm with its own price action have historically done better than the ones it has not, which is an ordinary momentum edge riding on an unusually curated, high-dispersion starting list.

card.thesis: AI-capex-cycle names re-rate on multi-quarter earnings-revision cycles, not single days: a data-center or cloud demand cycle shows up as a sequence of beat-and-raise quarters that institutional allocators scale into over months, not one print. That flow creates serial correlation in price that a same-day oscillator cannot see. The other side of the trade is investors who sell into strength too early, anchored to a pre-cycle 'fair value', and investors who panic-sell the first pullback inside an intact uptrend, mistaking noise for reversal -- both hand the rest of the move to a slower, rule-following holder. I measured this rather than assuming it: on this universe's last ~1500 sessions (~6y) through 2026-02-13, a close>sma(200) regime filter plus a 20/50-EMA crossover trigger produced 77 trades at 49.4% win rate, but average winners (+29.6%) were 4.1x average losers (-7.3%), and winning trades were held a median of 118 days vs 16 for losers -- the classic trend signature of a system that is right less than half the time and still profitable because it cuts losses fast and lets the rest run. The chop problem is real and I confronted it directly: the same golden-cross setup on this universe's smaller, more speculative names (IREN, OKLO, APLD, BE, KORU) produced negative average 60-day forward returns after the signal fired -- those names were excluded from the universe below specifically because the measured data showed the entries do not sustain here, not because of a prior. Within the chosen universe, widening the stop from 8% to 12% cut stop-outs from 12/77 (16%) to 7/77 (9%) while barely moving mean trade return (0.093->0.093), meaning most of the discarded stop-outs at the tighter level were noise, not real breakdowns -- direct evidence the wider stop survives chop without giving back the move. The regime filter (sma200) plus a medium-term trigger (ema20/50, not raw ema50/200) was chosen over a textbook dual-moving-average cross because it produces materially fewer whipsaw entries on this universe's large, liquid AI/semi/software names, at the cost of entering somewhat later into each trend.

card.thesis: Round 1 found that a short, sharp RSI(3)<15-and-close<bb_lower(10,2) dislocation in liquid semiconductor names resolved (closed back above ema(5)) in a median of 4 sessions with only 4.2% unresolved after 10 -- forced-flow selling exhausting itself fast, not a genuine repricing. Round 2 tests whether that speed is a semiconductor-specific quirk or a broad property of liquid index/sector baskets, using the same mechanism unchanged, over the same 2021-02-13 to 2026-02-13 window, on 24 candidate broad-index, sector, factor and international ETFs. It survives intact: median resolution across the strongest 12 candidates is still 3-4 sessions, with the same signal (rsi(3)<15, close<bb_lower(10,2)) firing 19-37 times per name -- speed is not a semiconductor property, it is a property of how liquid instruments absorb and clear forced selling, whether the forced seller is a single-stock stop cascade or an index-fund redemption wave. What differs from round 1, as the brief predicted, is amplitude, not speed: median bounce at the first ema(5) reclaim across this universe is roughly 1-2%, well under round 1's semis' 2.7-2.8%, because a basket has no single-company blow-up risk to overreact to and less of the multiple-expansion-and-compression that drives an outsized single-stock air-pocket. The other side of this trade is the same as round 1: index-fund flow and systematic de-risking extending a drawdown 1-3 sessions past where it settles, clearing into thin liquidity at the print, then unwinding as soon as the flow stops. The mechanically important finding is on sizing, not speed: I tested tightening stop_loss_pct/take_profit_pct down to match the smaller ETF bounce (e.g. 0.04/0.03) and it performs worse, not better -- a tight stop converts a dip that would have recovered on the ema(5) rule into a premature stop-out, since the engine evaluates stops off the previous close with next-open fills and cannot distinguish 'still resolving' from 'broken.' Keeping round 1's stop/take-profit (7%/5%) unchanged and letting the ema(5) rule do almost all of the work (in a 363-trade pooled simulation across the chosen 12 names, 331 of 363 exits, 91%, were the rule, only 4 were stops) produces a 69.4% win rate, mean win +1.62%, mean loss -1.82%, realized RRR approx 0.89 -- better than round 1's 0.71, because this universe's typical adverse excursion before resolving is small (median close-to-close drawdown during the hold was near zero to -1% for most names) even though its bounce is smaller too. A single large loss is still what erases this edge, and this universe adds a new version of that risk round 1's single-name semis did not have as acutely: same-day signal clustering. Because these are broad-market and sector proxies, the same broad-selloff day that dislocates SPY also dislocates 8-11 of the other 11 names simultaneously (verified on 2021-09-20, 2022-06-10, 2023-09-21 and five other dates) -- the 0.581 mean pairwise sector correlation this brief measured is exactly why. max_positions=6 at position_pct=0.15 (90% of book) caps how much of that pile-on the strategy can actually take, but it cannot prevent the remaining six positions from moving together if the broad drawdown continues past the median 3-4 session resolution window.

card.thesis: This engine cannot express relative strength: entry and exit are evaluated per symbol against that symbol's own bars, with no cross-sectional comparison, so there is no way to buy 'the strongest semiconductor name' or trade a spread. What this card actually does is apply one absolute condition -- close above its own 50-day average with RSI(14) between 55 and 80, i.e. a confirmed, non-extreme uptrend -- identically to a 9-name cyclical-semiconductor universe (NVDA AMD MU INTC MRVL AVGO TSM QCOM SOXX), and cap concurrent holdings at 3 of 9. That cap is the only 'rotation' logic available: the mechanism is that semiconductor demand and AI-capex cycles tend to move the whole group together and to persist for quarters rather than days, so entering only into names already confirmed in trend, and exiting on trend break or momentum fade, should keep capital on the right side of the cycle more often than not, while the cap prevents any single session from committing to more than 3 names at once. I measured pairwise daily-return correlation across these 9 names over the trailing ~253 sessions through 2026-02-13: mean 0.589, range 0.286 (INTC vs AVGO) to 0.824 (SOXX vs TSM). That is high -- this is a concentrated sector bet dressed as a 3-of-9 rotation, not a diversified basket, and I am not pretending otherwise. It is not a coin-flip between one name and nothing, though: breadth genuinely varies session to session under the proposed filter (median 4 of 9 names qualifying; at least 4 qualify on 50.6% of sessions, at least 6 on 21.3%), so the cap binds and actually forces a choice often enough to matter. When more than 3 names qualify on the same session, the broker fills entries in the fixed order the universe list is written -- alphabetical here -- not by any measure of relative strength, momentum magnitude, or liquidity. That is an arbitrary tiebreak, not a 'buy the leader' mechanism, and the card cannot do better than that. On the other side of these trades: momentum/trend traders who initiated the move earlier and are already positioned before this rule confirms it; mean-reversion sellers who fade strength too early inside a still-intact uptrend and get run over; and dip-buyers in choppy or declining regimes who buy bottoms this rule cannot see coming and will instead get chopped by.

card.thesis: Institutional flow into AI/cloud-infrastructure leaders re-rates them in slow, multi-week waves, not single days: a fund building a position over weeks pushes the medium-term average through the long-term one, and that crossover is a public, mechanical signal other trend-following capital reacts to next, extending the move further than any one participant intended. On the design-window history of these 12 names, once close > sma(200) is already established and ema(20) crosses above ema(50) -- a fresh acceleration inside a standing uptrend, not a bottom-pick -- the resulting move has a median duration of roughly 3-4 weeks and stretches past two months at the 75th percentile (NVDA's longest such run reached 256 sessions, MSFT's 169, TSM's 189). The other side of this trade is whoever sells into that strength: value-discipline holders trimming into a re-rate, and short sellers pressing a name that 'already ran too far' -- both wrong, on average, while the wave is still building. I tested a fixed take-profit and a fast rule exit against simply riding the position to a stop or a genuine trend break, on this same entry: capping gains at 8-30% cut mean per-signal return to 2-9%, and a fast 20-day-EMA exit (even with a 3-day confirmation filter) cut it to 3-5% and win rate to 42-49% by whipsawing out of live trends on ordinary pullbacks. Letting the position run to a stop, a 200-day trend-break, or a 180-day backstop produced roughly triple the aggregate return of either capped variant, at the cost of a median trade near breakeven-to-slightly-negative -- this strategy's edge is concentrated in a minority of large winners, which is exactly what a take-profit would have amputated. It is deliberately not diversified across volatility regimes: the universe was chosen so one stop and one position size fit all 12 names reasonably rather than being tuned to any single one.

card.thesis: Round 1's mechanism was post-shock drift: a true-range day well above its own ATR(14) that closes in the direction of the move is the market printing new information faster than participants can absorb it, and slow-moving capital re-rates the name over days rather than instantly. Round 2 asks whether that mechanism, and the comparable-volatility-cohort fix for the engine's single fixed stop_loss_pct/position_pct, survive leaving the sector I was forced into. I measured ATR(14)/close (trailing-252-session mean, same method as my round-1 card) across all 93 round-2 symbols through 2026-02-13: it spans 0.119% (SHY) to 4.137% (ARKG), roughly 35x -- and one name, SLV, is worth flagging on its own: its trailing mean is a moderate 2.908%, but its most recent single-day ATR/close is 13.2% because the design window ends inside what the bars show as a real short squeeze (SLV round-tripped roughly $67->$110->$69 in three weeks). That is event-driven, not persistent, vol -- exactly the kind a fixed stop should not be sized around. One correction to the round-2 brief's framing: measured this way, the round-2 spread (35x, or ~120x if SLV's last-day reading is used instead of its trailing mean) is actually narrower than round 1's 43-symbol spread (SGOV 0.035% to OKLO 10.513%, ~300x, matching the ~260x my round-1 card reported from rounded figures) -- so 'wider still' does not hold under my round-1 methodology applied consistently, though the underlying point (one stop cannot span either roster) is unaffected by which multiple it is. What round 2 actually adds is choice of cohort, not a bigger spread: I built a 6-symbol comparable-vol band -- TLT (0.979%), DBC (1.190%), EWJ (1.300%), XLU (1.465%), XLP (1.191%), INDA (0.969%) -- max/min ratio 1.51x, tighter than round 1's 1.6x, and this time drawn from four different macro drivers (long-duration US rates, a diversified commodity basket, Japanese and Indian equities, US utilities, US staples) instead of one semiconductor/momentum-tech sector. Pairwise daily-return correlation among these six (trailing 252 sessions): mean 21.7%, median 22.7%, max 50.4% (XLU-XLP), min -12.6% (TLT-DBC, genuinely negative) -- against my round-1 cohort's mean 48.8%, median 49.9%, max 72.1%, min 22.0%, all-positive. Comparable volatility without correlated exposure, which round 1's universe could not offer, is real and roughly halves both the average and the worst-case pairwise correlation while tightening the vol band slightly further. ATR/price persistence (lag-1 autocorrelation 0.98-0.99, lag-5 0.72-0.88 across the six) confirms these are multi-week vol regimes, not one-day noise, so an ATR-relative trigger is still measuring something real here. The one thing that did not transfer: round 1's exact entry (range > 1.5x ATR, close > open, close > sma(50)) fires 0-10 times per name per year on this cohort -- TLT and EWJ fired zero times in 252 sessions -- because index/bond ETFs absorb macro news continuously through arbitrage and duration-matched flow rather than producing the discrete, story-driven surprise days a single momentum stock does, and because sma(50) is a multi-month trend filter that fights a rates/carry-driven instrument's naturally choppier path. I dropped the sma(50) filter (it was measuring long-run direction, not the shock-absorption speed this discipline is about) and lowered the multiplier to 1.2x ATR, which restores 7-29 signals per name per year (85/year total across the six) while keeping the core condition: today's range must exceed its own recent typical range, and the session must close in the direction of the expansion. Stop and target are scaled from round 1's numbers by the ratio of mean ATR/price between the two cohorts (1.182% here vs 4.76% in round 1, a 0.25x factor): 10%->2.5% stop, 15%->3.75%(rounded to 4%) target, preserving the same ATR-multiple risk/reward geometry (RRR 1.5-1.6) rather than picking new round numbers. The counterparty on the other side of the trade is whoever is still transacting at the pre-shock price or NAV while the flow catches up: authorized participants and market makers absorbing creation/redemption lag, index rebalancers still executing against stale weights, or foreign-flow investors reacting to the same macro print a day late.
card.entry: high - low > atr(14) * 1.2 and close > open

card.thesis: Same mechanism as round 1: a Bollinger squeeze (band width under 8% of price) marks a name where buyers and sellers have reached a temporary truce, and a close back above the upper band out of that compression is the market resolving the truce in one direction, which systematic trend-following flow (CTAs, momentum funds, dealer hedging) then chases -- so a minority of breaks turn into extended continuation moves while the majority are false starts. The counterparty on a losing trade is whoever sold the breakout expecting immediate mean reversion and was right only briefly. What changes in round 2 is the universe and, because of it, the stop and the honesty about how thin the edge is. I redid the MAE stop study (my most careful round-1 work) on this cross-asset roster: across 1,367 squeeze-release signals on SPY/XLU/XLP/TLT/EFA/EEM/IBB/KRE/GDX (2003-2026 history, sma(20)-break-or-60-day exit, no stop), 0.0% of eventual winners ever retraced 4% or more from entry before their real exit -- the worst winner MAE in the whole sample was -3.9%. In round 1's semiconductor/AI universe a 5% stop cut over a quarter of eventual winners; here even a 3% stop only clips 0.4% of them. ETFs compress and release in smaller, shallower moves than single stocks, so I tightened the stop from round 1's 8% to 5% -- it costs essentially no winners here and meaningfully caps the loser tail, which single-stock-calibrated 8% would have left unnecessarily wide. I also checked the specific regime that broke the round-1 version: in round 1's universe, 2022 was 0% win rate across 5 trades, all in one correlated sector. On this diversified roster, 2022 produced 24 signals across 8 different symbols (XLU, XLP, SPY, TLT, EFA, EEM, IBB, KRE, GDX) at a 54.2% win rate and +0.79% mean return -- the semiconductor selloff that killed every round-1 signal simply didn't touch defensive sectors, long bonds, or EM equities compressing and releasing on their own schedules. That is the actual case for this round-2 card: not a stronger raw edge, but survival of a regime that was fatal to the concentrated version. I have to report the honest cost of that survival, though: aggregate profit factor across this roster is only ~1.00-1.04 (mean winner ~3.2%, mean loser ~-1.9%, win rate ~37%), roughly stable across sma-exit periods 15-30 and hold windows 40-90, versus round 1's ~1.35 on the same mechanism applied to higher-volatility single names. Diversification bought regime survival at the price of a much thinner raw edge -- close to breakeven before any transaction costs -- because ETF breakouts simply don't travel as far as single-stock breakouts. I measured correlations before assuming them: TLT/SPY correlation is 0.07 over the trailing 5 years (vs -0.31 over the full 2002-2026 history, a real regime shift toward positive stock-bond correlation since 2022's inflation shock) and GDX/SPY is 0.18-0.45 depending on window -- both genuinely low, which is the diversification this card is trying to buy. GDX earns its slot on that low correlation despite contributing 5 of the worst 10 trades in the entire sample from just 2% of signal count -- its squeezes are rarer (27 signals vs 100-236 for the others) and its releases gap harder than anything else in the roster, which the previous-close/next-open stop mechanic cannot fully contain.
card.entry: (bb_upper(20,2) - bb_lower(20,2)) < close * 0.08 and close crosses_above bb_upper(20,2)

card.thesis: Round 1's finding was that RENTECH (3,185 positions) and BRIDGEWATER (1,040) individually cover 51% and 63% of that roster and are barely more informative than a coin flip, so I built round 1's crowding score from the other 12 'selective' managers only, and even then found rho +0.17 to +0.25 at n~23-24, none significant, and refused to pick a direction. Round 2's instruction was explicit: establish real overlap before designing anything, and if crowding cannot be computed over enough names to mean anything, build a rotation strategy on measured correlations instead. I did the overlap measurement first. Method: for all 14 catalog managers filed by 2026-02-13 (as_of on filing date, never period, per the addendum), I pulled load_latest, applied catalog.apply_tickers via the ledger CUSIP bridge (119 CUSIPs resolvable, same bridge as round 1, unchanged), and intersected the resulting tickers against round 2's actual 93-symbol roster -- counted directly from the brief's own list (8 broad-equity + 10 sectors + 11 international + 8 bonds + 7 commodities + 7 factor/dividend + 13 thematic + 29 large-caps = 93; the large-cap section is explicitly headed 'AAPL-free list', so AAPL is not in the 93 despite appearing first in that line -- I initially miscounted 94 by including it, caught and corrected before finalizing this card). Result: of 5,071 raw holdings across all 14 managers (220 mapped to any ticker, the same 4.3% mapping rate as round 1, since the bridge is unchanged), exactly 4 holdings, spanning 3 distinct tickers, land on round 2's 93-symbol roster: IGV (BRIDGEWATER + RENTECH), XBI (RENTECH only), GDX (RENTECH only). Every single hit comes from the two megafunds round 1 already established are structurally uninformative -- RENTECH and BRIDGEWATER hold so much of the liquid market that their presence in a name is close to a base rate, not a selection signal. All 12 of the 'selective, independent' managers round 1's actual crowding score was built from -- BRK, PERSHING, APPALOOSA, DUQUESNE, THIRDPOINT, ELLIOTT, TIGERGLOBAL, COATUE, LONEPINE, SCION, ARKINVEST, SOROS -- contribute zero holdings to round 2's roster between them. That is not 'weaker than round 1', it is a different result in kind: round 1 had a genuine, if noisy, multi-manager count to correlate against returns (11-24 names, crowding scores 1-10). Round 2 has no such count at all -- there is no crowding score to build, because there is no overlapping name for the informative managers to disagree or agree about. Staleness makes it worse, not better: even RENTECH and BRIDGEWATER's own filings (Q4 2025, filed 2026-02-12/13, the freshest data available) describe positions 48 days old at trade start, and the other 10 managers' filings describe Q3-2025 positions 140 days stale -- but the staleness question is moot here since there is no usable overlap to be stale. Plain statement, as the brief asked for: 13F cannot reach this universe. I am not filtering a universe by crowding this round; there is nothing to filter with. What I did instead, per the brief's own fallback instruction, is verify the round-2 correlation table myself before leaning on it, and design a rotation strategy on what I actually measured. Over the trailing 259 sessions to 2026-02-13 I recomputed: IEF vs SPY -0.110 (exact match to the brief's figure), TLT vs SPY +0.090 (exact match), GLD vs SPY +0.042 (exact match) and its 24.9% annualised vol (exact match) -- though I note GLD is not actually in round 2's tradeable 93 (commodities are SLV USO DBC CPER PPLT GDX GDXJ, no GLD; the brief's own table cites a ticker outside the roster it hands out, which I flag rather than quietly work around), HYG vs SPY +0.824 (matches), EEM/FXI/EWZ vs SPY 0.74/0.52/0.49 (matches the stated 0.49-0.74 range), and the 10 round-2-eligible US sector ETFs' mean pairwise correlation at 0.576 (brief states 0.581 for 11 -- consistent, the extra name in their count is not in round 2's own sector list either). All verified, all confirmed. Since GLD is unavailable, I measured its round-2-eligible substitutes myself: SLV (52% ann. vol, 0.19/0.21 corr to SPY/QQQ), GDX/GDXJ (42%/47% vol, 0.21-0.26 corr, and 0.98 correlated with each other -- the same trade twice), USO (31% vol, 0.29/0.27 corr, 0.85 correlated with DBC -- redundant), CPER (37% vol, 0.36/0.35 corr), PPLT (45% vol, 0.12/0.14 corr). DBC (broad commodities: energy, ag and metals combined) was the best-balanced pick -- 16.6% vol, close enough to an equity engine's to share one fixed stop, and 0.35/0.34 corr to SPY/QQQ, a real but partial diversifier, not a clean one, and I am calling it that rather than overselling it the way the brief warned against for EM. For the rates leg, IEF has the single best number I measured (-0.110 SPY, -0.157 QQQ, 'a real diversifier' per the brief's own language) but only 5.6% annualised vol against QQQ's 23.2% -- a >4x spread that the engine's one global stop_loss_pct cannot serve honestly: a stop sized for QQQ would essentially never reach IEF, leaving it structurally unprotected against an actual duration shock, while a stop tight enough for IEF would shake QQQ out on ordinary noise. TLT (11.9% vol, +0.090/+0.037 corr to SPY/QQQ) is a weaker diversifier than IEF on paper but is 0.89 correlated with IEF itself -- the same rates factor -- so holding both is double-weighting one bet, not two, exactly the correlated-crowding mistake round 1 flagged in its own roster. I kept TLT alone: a real, verified low-correlation leg whose volatility the single stop can actually reach. I also dropped SPY as a second equity leg (0.971 correlated with QQQ -- the same trade twice again) and kept QQQ only, for its stronger measured trend behaviour. Final universe -- QQQ (growth/momentum engine), TLT (duration/rates), DBC (broad commodities) -- three distinct macro factors with mean pairwise correlation ~0.09 over the measured window (QQQ-TLT +0.04, QQQ-DBC +0.34, TLT-DBC -0.12), none of it the sector-ETF-in-eleven-costumes problem the brief warned about. Vol/signal stats measured at the cutoff: ATR14/close now vs 2yr-mean -- QQQ 1.92%/1.59% (1.20x, unremarkable), TLT 0.70%/1.04% (0.67x, currently calm), DBC 2.28%/1.18% (1.93x, elevated). I checked why: DBC's last 20 sessions show a steady six-session +1-2%/day rally in late January followed by a two-session pullback (-3.4%, -3.6%) in early February, worst single day in the trailing 60 sessions -3.64% -- a real move, not a crash, the same test round 1 applied to a GLD spike and this round's other risk-managed analyst applied to an XLU spike. Trailing-2-year entry-condition frequency: QQQ true 56.4% of days (39 new signals), TLT 21.8% (28 signals), DBC 31.8% (37 signals) -- TLT is the quietest leg, consistent with it being the true ballast. At the cutoff itself, entry is live on TLT and DBC but not QQQ (close 601.92 vs sma50 618.56, RSI 36.6, mid-pullback) -- a real, unfit-to illustration of the exact rotation the thesis claims: the growth leg's trend just broke while the two diversifying legs are independently trending. Stop/target sizing: trailing-2yr rolling-10-day worst-case drawdown (5th percentile) is QQQ -6.06%, TLT -4.19%, DBC -5.14%; stop_loss_pct=0.08 sits above all three so an ordinary bad stretch should not trip it under the engine's previous-close/next-open stop mechanics. take_profit_pct=0.16 (planned RRR 2.0). max_hold_days=120, close to the full 127-session trading window -- a backstop behind the rule exit and target, not the primary exit. Entry/exit rules are unchanged from round 1's mechanism (close > sma(50) and close > sma(150) and rsi(14) < 70 to enter; close < sma(50) or rsi(14) < 40 to exit) -- deliberately reused rather than reinvented, because it is a generic trend-confirm/trend-break rule already vetted once, and SMA/RSI are relative, percentage-scale measures that translate reasonably across QQQ, TLT and DBC's very different price levels and vol regimes; reusing a known mechanism on a genuinely new universe is a discipline against fitting a second rule to a second dataset. max_positions=3, position_pct=0.33 (0.99 total) -- one slot per leg, all three can be held at once, because simultaneous holding across low-correlation legs is the actual diversification claim under test, not something to size around. Mechanism: applying an identical trend rule to three macro-uncorrelated instruments means capital rotates to whichever leg is genuinely trending; when the growth leg's trend breaks in a risk-off move, the duration and commodity legs' entries are not mechanically tied to the same trigger, and over the measured window they were in fact low/negatively correlated to it, so the book has a chance to be allocated somewhere still working rather than drawn down uniformly. On the other side of every fill: momentum traders already positioned before the confirmation filter, and macro allocators rotating out of duration or commodities into growth exactly as this strategy rotates the other way. What changed from round 1: everything except the entry/exit mechanism. Round 1 was a single-asset-class (mega-cap tech), 13F-filtered momentum screen inside a semiconductor/AI-heavy roster; round 2 has zero usable 13F signal on the new roster (measured, not assumed) and is a three-factor cross-asset rotation built entirely from price data and verified correlations -- the opposite kind of universe and the opposite edge claim (structural diversification, not smart-money convergence). What I expect to go wrong: (1) correlation instability -- a matrix measured over one mostly-calm 259-session window is not a structural law, and in a genuine liquidity event (a 2022-style simultaneous equity/bond selloff, or a commodity dislocation) these correlations can move toward 1 exactly when the diversification is needed, with no mechanism here to detect the regime shift ahead of price. (2) A prolonged choppy market across all three legs would generate repeated small stop-outs and re-entries independently on each -- ordinary trend-following whipsaw, now paid three times over instead of once. (3) DBC's 0.34-0.35 correlation to equities is real, not zero; in a global growth-scare it could sell off with QQQ rather than diversify it, leaving only TLT doing the diversifying job the thesis claims for two legs. (4) The single global 8% stop spans a vol range of 0.70%-2.28% ATR even after deliberately dropping IEF to narrow that spread -- it is a compromise, not the per-name risk control a single-asset-class card can offer, and I am stating that mismatch rather than pretending three legs also solved it.

card.thesis: A true-range day 1.5x its own ATR(14) is the market printing new information faster than participants can absorb it -- an earnings reaction, a guidance change, a sector-wide repricing. When that expansion day also closes above open and above the 50-day trend, the imbalance is more likely a repricing that continues than a one-day panic that mean-reverts: momentum research (e.g. post-earnings drift) shows large-surprise days keep drifting for weeks because slow-moving capital (index funds, institutions with review cycles, retail attention) re-rates the name over days rather than instantly. The counterparty is whoever sells into that expansion bar at the old price because they have not yet re-priced the new information, or is forced to sell into the move on a stop or a mandate -- both hand the follow-through to whoever holds after the bar closes. This is genuinely a volatility-discipline: the trigger is range relative to ATR, not a moving-average cross or an oversold oscillator, so it is selecting for the size of the move as well as its direction. The engine's structural weakness for this discipline is that stop_loss_pct and position_pct are single numbers with no per-symbol ATR scaling, so I measured ATR-to-price across the full 43-symbol universe through 2026-02-13 and it spans roughly 0.04% (SGOV) to 10.5% (OKLO) -- a ~260x range in which one stop cannot fit both ends. Rather than accept that mismatch, I built a 12-symbol universe (NVDA, AMD, MU, INTC, MRVL, DELL, AVGO, TSLA, COIN, NET, SNOW, PLTR) whose trailing-year ATR/price ratios cluster tightly between 3.68% and 5.98% (mean 4.76%, max/min ratio 1.6x, versus 260x for the full list) -- comparable-enough volatility that one stop and one size are a defensible approximation rather than a silent lie the thesis pretends isn't there. I deliberately excluded the very-low-vol cash/bond/gold names (SGOV, AGG, GLD, SCHD -- ATR/price under 2%, where a 10% stop is nearly un-hittable noise) and the extreme-vol small caps (IREN, APLD, OKLO, NBIS, BE, CRDO, SNDK -- ATR/price above 6.5%, where a 10% stop is routine chop) for the same reason. ATR/price also persists strongly in this universe (lag-1 autocorrelation 0.94-0.99, lag-5 0.79-0.94 across all 43 names, measured through 2026-02-13) -- volatility regimes here are not one-day noise, they cluster for weeks, which is what makes an ATR-relative trigger meaningful rather than arbitrary.

card.display_name: Cross-Asset Trend Sleeve (13F Bridge Failed on This Roster)
card.thesis: Round 2 opens with a measurement, not a strategy: how many of the 93-symbol roster can 13F actually name here. I re-ran the exact scan round 1 used -- all 14 tracked managers (BRK, PERSHING, APPALOOSA, DUQUESNE, THIRDPOINT, ELLIOTT, TIGERGLOBAL, COATUE, LONEPINE, SCION, ARKINVEST, RENTECH, SOROS, BRIDGEWATER), each fund's latest filing public as of the 2026-02-13 cutoff (as_of enforced on every call) -- and checked every holding's resolved ticker against this round's roster instead of round 1's. Total holdings across all 14 books: 5,071. Holdings that resolved to any ticker at all (the ledger CUSIP bridge working at all): 220 (4.3%, in line with round 1). Holdings that resolved to a ticker on the round-2 roster: 4 -- 0.08% of 5,071, effectively the zero the brief warned this would be close to. All 4 came from RENTECH (3 hits: XBI cusip 78464A870 weight 0.0078%, GDX cusip 92189F106 weight 0.0059%, IGV cusip 464287515 weight 0.0049%, out of RENTECH's 3,185 positions) and BRIDGEWATER (1 hit: IGV cusip 464287515 weight 0.1087%, out of BRIDGEWATER's 1,040 positions). Both funds were the two I excluded on their face in round 1 for having so many positions that no single line can represent a real bet -- RENTECH's three hits each sit below even RENTECH's own 1/3185=0.031% equal-weight bar (0.0078% and 0.0059% and 0.0049% are all smaller), so by my own round-1 methodology none clears the 'this is actually overweighted' test. BRIDGEWATER's IGV hit does clear its 1/1040=0.096% equal-weight bar (0.109% vs 0.096%, about 1.13x), the one technically-overweight line in the whole scan -- but BRIDGEWATER is a risk-parity macro fund holding 1,040 positions, and the one hit is an iShares software-ETF share, not a single company Bridgewater has a stock-picking view on; an ETF holding inside a systematic macro book identifies no issuer to buy and cannot seed a single-name universe entry even nominally. So: zero of 5,071 holdings across every manager this repo tracks give a defensible, conviction-weighted, single-name mapping onto this round's roster. I am not asserting any CUSIP-to-ticker mapping in this card -- there is nothing here that clears the bar the brief sets for asserting one. 13F is not usable on this roster, full stop, and that is on top of round 1's separate finding that even where the bridge did work, the signal itself was bad: round 1's 8-name conviction basket (built from PERSHING and APPALOOSA overweights, the only two managers that mapped meaningfully) returned -3.93% from filing date to the design cutoff, against +10.13% for the equal-weighted 43-symbol roster and -1.13% for QQQM, and Scion's largest position by disclosed weight was Palantir PUTS, not a bullish stake -- a reminder that even a working ticker map can point the wrong direction. Two independent failures of the same signal, on two different rosters, is enough; this card carries zero 13F input and is not designed to look like it does. What round 2 does instead is use the thing it uniquely offers that round 1's forced 43-name, semiconductor-crowded universe could not: real cross-asset diversification. I measured 259-session pairwise correlation and annualized volatility through the cutoff across a shortlist of 24 round-2 candidates spanning equity, duration, credit, gold, broad commodities and factor tilts, and it corroborates the brief's own table rather than contradicting it: SPY-vs-IEF -0.110, SPY-vs-TLT 0.090, SPY-vs-GLD 0.042 are genuinely near-zero-or-negative, while the assets that look diversifying by label are not -- XLU 0.470, USMV 0.749, HYG 0.824, EEM 0.738 vs SPY all ride substantially the same equity beta the brief flagged. I additionally measured DBC (broad commodities), not in the brief's table: 0.347 vs SPY (moderate, well below the sector-ETF or EM levels), -0.225 vs IEF (genuinely anti-correlated to duration), and 0.478 vs GLD (related to gold's real-asset trade but not the same instrument -- GDX-vs-GLD at 0.820 and SLV-vs-GLD at 0.747 show what 'basically the same trade wearing a different ticker' actually looks like, and DBC is not that). The universe is four names, each representing a return driver this data shows is not the same trade as the others: SPY (US equity beta), IEF (intermediate Treasuries), GLD (gold), DBC (broad commodities). The largest of the six pairwise correlations among these four is 0.478 (GLD-DBC); the other five are all below 0.35 and three are near zero or negative. Compare that to round 1's own semiconductor cluster (mean pairwise 0.589, per this brief) or this round's 11 US sector ETFs (mean pairwise 0.581) -- this basket is not that. Entry and exit rules deliberately reuse round 1's trend-confirmation structure -- close above both the 50- and 200-day average, RSI capped under 70 so entries are not chased into an already-extended move, exit on a break of the 50-day average -- not because 13F informs it (it does not; this card has no 13F input anywhere) but because round 1 already showed that gating on confirmed trend rather than buying blind is the more defensible rule on its own merits, independent of what selects the universe. Risk sizing: I measured ATR(14)/close at the cutoff for all four names -- SPY 1.32%, GLD 4.58%, DBC 2.28%, IEF 0.34%. The card's single 8% stop is about 6.1x SPY's ATR, 1.75x GLD's, and 3.5x DBC's -- reasonable, not noise-width, for three of four legs. For IEF it is roughly 23.5x ATR, effectively inert: IEF's own daily noise will essentially never trip an 8% stop, so in practice its downside control comes from the trend-break exit and the time stop, not stop_loss_pct. I am naming that mismatch rather than hiding it, per the brief's instruction on single fixed stops across mixed-volatility universes -- and I judge it acceptable rather than a defect, because tightening the shared stop to fit IEF's 0.34% ATR would whipsaw the other three legs out of ordinary daily noise, which is worse than leaving IEF's stop functionally unused. max_positions=4 at position_pct=0.20 commits at most 80% of the book, an explicit 20% cash buffer appropriate to a risk-managed card built on a signal (institutional conviction) I have now shown does not survive contact with this data twice. take_profit_pct=0.16 keeps a 2:1 planned reward:risk. max_hold_days=120 gives slower cross-asset trends -- gold and broad commodities move on a longer clock than semiconductors -- most of the ~six-month window to develop while still forcing resolution before TRADE_END, so an open position at the end is not left uncounted.
