card.thesis: Round 1 forced this discipline into one sector; round 2 lets me test its central weakness directly -- trend following's worst outcome is not a bad trade, it is every position turning at once, which is a correlation problem before it is a signal problem. I measured correlation rather than assumed it. Trailing 2y (504-session) daily-return correlation across my round-1 universe (NVDA AVGO TSM ORCL SOXX NFLX MU META QCOM) averages 0.501 pairwise (median 0.468, range 0.219-0.800) through 2026-02-13 -- nine names sharing one regime. The round-2 roster this card actually trades (NVDA MU GDX EWZ FXI INDA DBC) averages 0.274 pairwise over the same window, a ~45% reduction, with every pair outside the NVDA/MU core below 0.39 and GDX the most decoupled name in the set (0.16-0.22 vs NVDA/MU). But correlation alone is not sufficient, and I tested that too: I ran the identical unscaled rule (close>sma(200) & ema(20)-crosses-above-ema(50) entry, ema(20)-crosses-below-ema(50) exit, 12% stop, 120-day time stop -- same parameters as my round-1 card, same trailing ~1500-session/6y design methodology) on every 'obvious diversifier' round 2 exposes. Bonds (TLT, mean trade return -1.6% over 5 trades), utilities (XLU, -0.5% over 18 trades), regional banks (KRE, -0.8%), biotech (XBI, -0.2%), copper (CPER, -1.1%) and defence (ITA, +2.2% mean but only 28.6% win rate, and 0.53 correlated to the semis sleeve -- a worse diversifier than gold despite the label) all showed flat-to-negative or too-thin edge under this exact rule to earn a slot: including them would not have reduced correlated drawdown, it would have parked capital in dead-or-negative-expectancy positions that still occasionally fire a badly-timed entry. Gold miners (GDX) were the standout: 4 trades in 6y, 75% win rate, +20.9% mean trade return, lowest correlation to the core of anything tested. Brazil (EWZ, +2.1% mean trade, 0.23-0.30 corr), China (FXI, +2.8%, 0.24-0.31 corr), India (INDA, +4.5%, 0.21-0.26 corr, only 0.07 correlated to DBC) and broad commodities (DBC, +5.5%, 0.07-0.39 corr) all cleared a lower but genuinely positive bar and are the five diversifying sleeves in this universe. NVDA and MU stay as the trend engine because that is where the measured edge is largest -- +17.3% and +20.6% mean trade return respectively in the same 6y window, against +12.7% averaged across all nine round-1 names and +9.7% averaged across this seven-name diversified book. The mechanism is unchanged from round 1: gradual institutional flow into a confirmed uptrend, plus both premature profit-taking and panicked pullback-selling handing the rest of a move to a slower, rule-following holder -- but now spread across sleeves whose macro drivers are structurally different (US AI capex cycle, gold's real-rate/dollar cycle, EM equity flows, broad commodity demand), so a single regime turning cannot take out the whole book the way it structurally can in a one-sector universe. This is a real trade-off, not a free lunch: the diversified book's measured per-trade expectancy (9.7%) is lower than the concentrated book's (12.7%) on this identical rule and sample -- I am spending some expected return to buy a reduction in simultaneous-drawdown risk, and round 1 is the direct comparison for whether that trade was worth it. Realised 2y annualised volatility on this universe ranges from INDA (14.1%) to MU (60.0%), a 4.3x spread wider than round 1's uniformly high-vol semis cluster, exactly as the brief warned. I did not rescale the single 12% stop because the engine cannot: it is proportionately tight on NVDA/MU (12.5%-25% measured stop-hit rate in the design window) and proportionately loose on INDA/DBC/EWZ/FXI (0% measured stop-hit rate over the same window) -- I am stating that mismatch rather than pretending a single number fits both a 60%-vol stock and a 14%-vol commodity ETF equally well.
card.entry: close > sma(200) and ema(20) crosses_above ema(50)

card.thesis: A name still trading above its 200-day average that prints a fresh RSI(14)<30 reading is absorbing short-horizon, sentiment-driven selling (an earnings wobble, a sector rotation, a macro scare) on top of intact longer-horizon demand -- not a repricing of the business. The counterparty is short-term momentum sellers and forced sellers (stop cascades, vol-targeting funds cutting exposure into the drawdown) selling at peak discomfort; the trade is that once that flow exhausts, the buyers already accumulating the name near its 200dma step back in and close the gap. RSI(14) crossing back above 50 is the empirical marker that the flow has turned (median 9 sessions in-sample), which is why the exit is a rule rather than a fixed target -- the thesis is about waiting for evidence selling has stopped, not capturing a fixed move. This directly confronts mean-reversion's structural failure mode: buying oversold in a name that is simply falling. Measured on the full 43-symbol universe through 2026-02-13 (RSI(14) crossing below 30, n=1990 signals over 8+ years), requiring close>sma(200) at signal (n=247) vs not (n=1743) raised the 10-day win rate from 55.3% to 61.1% and cut the average further adverse move over the next 10 days from -5.55% to -4.18% -- a real but modest effect, not a cure. Breaking that trend-filtered set down by symbol showed the semiconductor/AI-infrastructure cyclicals do not actually mean-revert even with the filter on: MU (n=8, mean 10d fwd -7.6%, 12.5% win), EWY (n=3, -8.6%, 0%), INTC (n=15, -2.9%, 40%), DELL (n=8, -2.8%, 37.5%), ORCL (n=13, -2.6%, 38.5%), NVDA (n=11, -0.4%, 54.5%) -- an oversold reading in these names was more often the first leg of a larger decline than a bounce, i.e. exactly the trap this discipline dies to, hiding inside a universe-level average that looked fine. I therefore excluded them. Eight names showed a genuine, if noisy, edge under the same filter: ADBE (n=14, +5.0%, 85.7% win), UNH (n=14, +5.3%, 64.3%), META (n=7, +5.5%, 71.4%), TSM (n=6, +4.6%, 83.3%), NFLX (n=10, +4.6%, 70%), GOOGL (n=14, +1.0%, 71.4%), QCOM (n=10, +1.4%, 60%), MSFT (n=11, +0.7%, 63.6%) -- combined 86 signals, mean 10-day forward return +3.4% (70.9% win), mean 20-day +4.0% (67.4% win), RSI(14) recovering above 50 within 20 sessions 72% of the time (median 9 sessions). Adverse excursion over the 20 sessions after entry: median -2.6%, 25th pct -6.7%, 10th pct -13.9%, 5th pct -17.8%; a 10% stop would have fired on ~16% of signals, catching the real washout-that-doesn't-turn tail without sitting inside the typical -3% to -7% pullback that produces the signal (mean washout depth from the trailing 20-day high at entry was -14.5%, so a tighter stop would fire on the setup itself). I also checked volatility comparability since the engine's stop_loss_pct/position_pct are single fixed numbers: trailing-120-day annualized return vol for the eight chosen names clusters 25.4%-40.9% (ATR/price 3.3%-4.7%), a ~1.6x band. I excluded SCHD/BRK.B (11.3%/13.6% ann vol) because a 10% stop is nearly unhittable there and their filtered signal count was thin (11, 16) anyway, and excluded AVGO/MRVL/AMD (49%-68% ann vol) because a 10% stop is closer to noise-width at that volatility, despite attractive-looking but tiny samples (n=3, 7, 12).
card.entry: rsi(14) crosses_below 30 and close > sma(200)

card.thesis: Round 1 (43-symbol user universe) found RSI(14) oversold-in-uptrend (close>sma(200)) has a real but split edge: mega-cap software/services (ADBE, MSFT, META, GOOGL, TSM, QCOM, NFLX, UNH; 86 signals) mean-reverted cleanly (10d fwd +3.4%, 70.9% win; 20d +4.0%, 67.4% win), while semiconductor/AI-infrastructure cyclicals kept falling after the same signal (MU n=8, 10d -7.6%, 12.5% win; INTC n=15, -2.9%, 40% win). Round 2's mandate was to test that split directly against index and sector ETFs, on the reasoning that a basket diversifies away the single-headline blow-up that turns 'oversold' into 'still falling' -- a sector or index cannot go to zero on one earnings miss the way a stock can. I measured it rather than assumed it. Re-running the identical signal (rsi(14) crosses_below 30 and close>sma(200), same design window through 2026-02-13) on 6 broad-market cap-weighted index ETFs (SPY, QQQ, DIA, IWM, VTV, VUG) produced 71 signals: 10-day forward +1.71% (70.0% win), 20-day forward +2.41% (78.6% win) -- win rates that beat even round 1's best single-stock cluster, with a downside tail that is dramatically shallower: median adverse excursion over the following 20 sessions was -0.79% and 10th-percentile adverse was -5.19%, versus -2.57%/-13.85% for round 1's good-stock cluster and, on a fresh same-methodology recheck of a semiconductor/high-beta cluster (MU, NVDA, INTC, AVGO, TSLA, AMD, SOXX; 59 signals, 10d +0.8%/50.9% win, 20d +2.4%/54.2% win), -7.69%/-20.14%. Only 7.0% of the broad-index signals breached -8% at any point in the 20 sessions after entry. On this evidence baskets do revert more cleanly than single stocks, by a wide margin, not a marginal one. That result is not uniform across all baskets, though, which matters for universe choice: I also tested the 10 single-sector SPDRs and two non-cap-weighted broad variants (RSP equal-weight S&P, MDY mid-cap). Sector SPDRs pooled to a much weaker 57.1%/65.5% win rate (10d/20d, n=84) and one reproduced the exact single-stock trap this discipline dies to -- XLY (consumer discretionary) oversold-in-uptrend readings kept falling rather than bouncing (n=11, 10d -3.2%/27.3% win, 20d -1.4%/54.5% win), the same failure mode as MU/INTC in round 1, just less extreme because it is spread across ~50 names instead of one. RSP and MDY were also weaker than the cap-weighted benchmarks (RSP n=10: 10d +0.4%/60% win, 20d -1.0%/50% win; MDY n=12: 10d +0.2%/58.3%, 20d +0.9%/66.7%) -- equal-weighting and mid-cap both reintroduce some of the idiosyncratic dispersion a cap-weighted broad index diversifies away. I excluded all of these and built the universe from the six cleanest cap-weighted broad benchmarks only. Mechanism: a broad or large-cap-style index selling off to RSI<30 while still above its 200dma is, almost by construction, a market-wide risk-off flush -- vol-targeting funds cutting gross exposure, systematic de-risking, a macro scare -- rather than a repricing of hundreds of individual businesses at once. The counterparty is the same short-horizon forced-seller flow round 1's thesis relied on, but the object being sold is beta itself, and beta's long-run demand (401k flows, pension rebalancing, systematic dip-buying) is more mechanical and reliable than any single company's buyer base, which is why one bad headline cannot invalidate the setup the way it can for a stock. Exit and sizing were set from the same design-window data. RSI(14) recovered above 50 within 40 sessions for 70/71 signals (98.6%), median 11 sessions, mean 13; at that exit the mean realized return was +2.48% (88.6% win), a materially higher win rate than either fixed-horizon check because the rule times the exit to the actual recovery. max_hold_days=40 is a backstop for the one signal that never recovered; I skipped a take-profit because at a 12% threshold zero of 71 signals ever reached it before the rsi(14) exit fired, so a fixed target would be inert on this universe and I did not want a field implying work it measurably does not do. stop_loss_pct=0.08 sits below the typical noise of the setup (median 20-day adverse -0.79%, 25th pct -2.67%) but above all but the worst ~7% tail. Unlike round 1, the six symbols share a genuinely tight trailing-120-day annualized-vol band (SPY 11.4%, QQQ 15.9%, IWM 18.6%, DIA 11.2%, VTV 10.0%, VUG 15.5% -- 10.0%-18.6%, a 1.9x range), so one fixed stop is not stretched thin the way it would be pairing a bond ETF with a leveraged single name. One honest limitation: these six ETFs are not independent bets. Trailing-3-year daily-return correlations run 0.64-0.98 pairwise (QQQ-VUG 0.98, SPY-QQQ 0.95, DIA-VTV 0.92 on the high end; VTV-VUG 0.64 on the low end) because they are all, fundamentally, US equity beta sliced different ways; max_positions/position_pct here controls capital exposure to a single market-wide flush, not diversification across uncorrelated return streams. I considered adding a non-equity basket (GLD, TLT) for genuine diversification now that round 2 allows it, and rejected it: the mechanism above is specifically about equity beta's forced-seller/dip-buyer dynamic, while gold or long bonds mean-revert, if at all, on a different macro driver entirely -- bolting one symbol from a different asset class onto this card would not diversify this strategy's bet, it would quietly run a second, unmeasured strategy inside the same card. Universe is ordered by measured 20-day win rate (DIA 93.3%, VTV 87.5%, QQQ 81.8%, SPY 73.3%, VUG 70.0%, IWM 63.6%) since round 2 confirmed that order is the tiebreak when more names signal than max_positions allows.

card.thesis: Round 1 found that on a concentrated AI/semiconductor megacap universe, this entry (ema(20) crosses_above ema(50) while close is already above sma(200) -- a fresh acceleration confirmed inside a standing uptrend, not a bottom-pick) produces a positive mean per-trade return concentrated almost entirely in a minority of large winners: the median trade sits near breakeven-to-negative, so a take-profit would amputate the only part of the distribution doing the work. This round tests whether that is a single-stock artifact -- one company's earnings beat or FDA approval -- that a sector/thematic basket, driven by slower institutional flow rather than one firm's news cycle, would smooth into a gentler payoff. Measured directly, it is not. I ran the identical entry/exit through 2026-02-13 against all eight tickers this round's brief named (SMH IGV XBI ITA KRE JETS TAN ICLN) plus IBB, GDX, GDXJ, EWZ and TLT as candidate diversifiers. On the seven that survived to the final universe (SMH IGV XBI ITA TAN GDX EWZ, 174 historical signals): median trade return -1.93%, mean +6.74%, win rate 34% -- both figures essentially unchanged from round 1's -2.15% median / +13.8% mean, and the win rate is lower than round 1's 41%, not higher. The skew is, if anything, sharper here: TAN's entire positive contribution rides on a 12% win rate with one +241% trade; GDX and EWZ's positive means are each carried by one or two multi-month legs (max trades of +103% and +86%) against a majority of small stopped-out losses. Capping gains confirms the mechanism directly: a 12% take-profit cuts the aggregate sum of trade returns across this universe from 11.73 to 4.17 (-64%); even a generous 30% cap still gives up 45% of it (11.73 -> 6.50), and the median stays negative under every cap level tested, because a cap clips exactly the tail carrying the mean. A sector rotation does not replace single-name catalyst risk with a gentler payoff on this evidence -- it replaces earnings/FDA-type binary risk with macro/flow-type binary risk (a rate-cut repricing regional banks, a subsidy headline repricing solar, a rate/dollar move repricing miners), and that risk is exactly as lumpy. No take-profit, again, deliberately, on measured evidence rather than a carried-over assumption. What I did differently with the open universe: I stopped assuming 'sector ETF' means 'diversified' and measured pairwise daily-return correlation on the design window instead of the category label. KRE and JETS were dropped -- under this specific entry they produce a near-zero-to-negative mean and win rate (regional banks and airlines chop more than they form a clean ema(20)/ema(50)/sma(200) acceleration on this history). ICLN correlates at 0.88 with TAN in this window -- almost the same trade under two tickers -- so I kept TAN (longer history, stronger individual mean: 0.163 vs 0.104) and dropped ICLN; IBB correlates at 0.92 with XBI for the same reason and lost out to XBI's better win rate. TLT, tested as a bond-momentum leg, failed outright on this entry (mean -0.7%, win rate 26%, no real tail) -- an EMA-cross trend-acceleration signal does not describe how a rate-driven instrument moved in this window, so I did not force a bond sleeve into a card built around trend breakouts just because round 2 made bonds available. GDX and EWZ earned their slots on both a real edge under this entry (mean +6.9%/+8.1%, tail-carried like everything else here) and genuine correlation reduction: GDX runs at 0.18-0.34 against the other six names, the one real outlier in the book; EWZ sits at a more moderate 0.34-0.60. Net effect: the final seven-name basket's average pairwise correlation is 0.48, down from the eight-symbol thematic set's 0.55 -- which was, contrary to my prior assumption, higher than round 1's semiconductor/megacap correlation of 0.45; sector ETFs are not automatically less correlated than single growth stocks. 0.48 is a modest, not dramatic, improvement on round 1: six of these seven names are still equity beta sharing a risk-on/risk-off factor, and GDX alone is doing the real diversification work. The other side of this trade: trend-following capital piling in once the crossover confirms, extending the move further than any one buyer intended -- round 1's mechanism, unchanged. On the diversifiers specifically, the other side is whoever is still selling GDX into a real breakout on a 'gold miners are a value trap' prior, or fading EWZ on stale Brazil political-risk headlines while the flow (US rate-cut expectations, commodity terms of trade) has already turned. What I expect to go wrong: a broad risk-off flush that stops out every open position in the same week regardless of each name's own trend, since these seven correlate far more on sharp down days than the 0.18-0.60 range measured here on ordinary days -- tail correlation in a systemic drawdown is exactly what a benign two-year design window cannot have tested. A close second: a rangebound, low-dispersion regime across sectors that never lets ema(20) separate cleanly from ema(50), which starves the strategy of the acceleration signal it needs and produces nothing but the small stopped-out losses that make up the median trade -- described, not fixed, by design.

card.thesis: A Bollinger squeeze (band width under 8% of price) marks a name where buyers and sellers have reached a temporary truce while they wait on a catalyst -- in this semiconductor/AI-capex-heavy universe that catalyst is usually an earnings print, a guidance revision, or a capacity/order headline. When price closes back above the upper band out of that compression, it is the market resolving the truce in one direction. The edge is not a high hit rate: it is that systematic trend-following flow (CTAs, momentum funds, dealer hedging) chases the resolved direction once it is confirmed, so a minority of breaks turn into extended continuation moves, while the majority are false starts that get run over by the same flow reversing. The counterparty on a losing trade is the trader who sold the breakout expecting mean reversion back into the range and was right only briefly. I measured this directly (see report): squeeze-then-close-above-band signals across 11 comparable-volatility names in this universe show a 36% win rate over a 60-session hold with a quick SMA(20) trend-break exit, mean winner +8.5% against mean loser -3.5% (profit factor ~1.35), and that ratio held up across a range of stop widths (6-10%), hold windows (40-90 sessions) and exit-SMA periods (10-30) rather than depending on one tuned combination -- so the strategy is built to survive on a few large winners paying for many small ones, not to be right often.

card.thesis: Capital preservation comes first here, so the design choice that matters most is which two names to own, not how cleverly to time them. I measured daily range, ATR14, and cross-correlation across the whole low-volatility candidate set (SGOV, AGG, GLD, SCHD, BRK.B) plus the book's existing AI/semiconductor names as of 2026-02-13, and concentrated in just SCHD and BRK.B rather than spreading across the wider universe -- because every other 'calm' candidate had a specific, measured reason to be excluded, not a marginal one. SGOV moves an average of 0.01% a day (2024-2026): there is no signal to trade, only a cash substitute. AGG's ATR14 (~0.39% of close) is roughly a third of SCHD/BRK.B's (1.1-1.7%), so one shared stop_loss_pct is either noise-width on AGG or absurdly loose on the other two -- the exact single-fixed-stop mismatch this tournament's engine cannot express around. GLD is the most surprising exclusion: its 2-year average ATR14 is 1.25% of close, squarely in the 'calm' band, but as of the design cutoff its ATR14 had spiked to 4.58% -- almost 4x its own norm -- after a -10.3% one-session move on 2026-01-29/30, three weeks before cutoff. That is a live regime break, not routine chop, and a stop sized for GLD's history would not fit GLD's present. UNH carries a documented -22% single-session move in this same window (a gap no previous-close stop can catch). And QQQM, despite calm absolute volatility, correlates 0.76 with NVDA and 0.67 with MU in the design window -- it is not diversification from this book's AI/semiconductor concentration, it is more of the same factor. SCHD and BRK.B, by contrast, sit in a tight, comparable ATR14 band (1.1-1.7%), correlate near zero with NVDA/MU (0.04-0.30), and correlate only 0.62 with each other -- genuinely different businesses (dividend-equity index vs. insurance/utility/cash-rich conglomerate) that happen to share a volatility regime. The entry itself buys a resumption, not a breakout: price above both its 50- and 200-day averages (the primary and intermediate trend must already be up), RSI reset into a neutral 40-60 band (not overbought, not a falling knife), and price reclaiming its 10-day EMA -- i.e., a shallow pullback within an established uptrend has just stabilized. The other side of this trade is momentum traders who chased the prior leg and flinched on the pullback, and dip-buyers who bought too early and got shaken out before the reset was confirmed; this rule deliberately gives up the first leg of a move to buy the second leg once trend-following capital has re-asserted control, which is a return given up for a lower chance of holding a broken trend. The 8% stop is not tight: it sits at roughly 4.8-6x each name's current ATR14 and above the measured 90th-percentile worst 10-day rolling drawdown for both names (SCHD 5.7%, BRK.B 7.3%), so ordinary daily or weekly noise should not trip it under the engine's previous-close stop rule -- a stop-out here should mean the trend actually broke, not that a routine down day printed. The 8% target and 90-session hold are sized off historical hit-rate tests of this exact rule since 2020: results differ by name (reported honestly, not smoothed over) -- BRK.B: 54 signals, 29 hit target vs 3 hit stop, 81.5% win rate, average +4.8% per trade; SCHD: 64 signals, 16 hit target vs 18 hit stop, 53.1% win rate, average -0.16% per trade, roughly flat. Both are reported because a risk-managed strategy should be judged on whether losers are actually controlled, not on which single number looks best.

card.thesis: Round 1 forced a two-name book (SCHD, BRK.B) because every other calm candidate in that universe had a specific disqualifying property -- that was concentration, not diversification, and I said so at the time. Round 2's roster genuinely offers what round 1 could not: sleeves that do not move together. I measured ATR14-as-%-of-close, daily-return correlation, and rolling 10-day drawdown percentiles over the trailing 2 years (2024-02-13 to 2026-02-13) across the full low-volatility candidate set handed to me -- SHY, MUB, BND, TIP, LQD, IEF, TLT, USMV, SPLV, VIG, DVY, XLP, XLU -- plus HYG as a comparison-only name, and the correlation matrix splits cleanly into two clusters. Government/investment-grade bonds (SHY, MUB, BND, TIP, LQD, IEF, TLT) correlate 0.58-0.98 with each other -- one rates factor wearing seven tickers. Equity low-volatility/dividend names (USMV, SPLV, VIG, DVY, XLP, XLU) correlate 0.48-0.90 with each other -- one defensive-equity factor wearing six more. But across the two clusters, correlation drops to 0.08-0.41 (e.g. TLT-VIG 0.15, TLT-USMV 0.21, IEF-VIG 0.08, SHY-DVY 0.15) -- these are genuinely different bets, not the same trade twice. I also measured LQD vs HYG specifically, since the brief named that pair: LQD correlates 0.88-0.94 with the Treasury sleeve (it trades on rates, like the brief said credit funds can) while HYG correlates only 0.40 with TLT/IEF but 0.55-0.75 with the equity-defensive sleeve (USMV 0.64, VIG 0.75, DVY 0.69) -- HYG is a credit fund that behaves like equity risk, not a hedge against it, which is exactly the LQD-vs-HYG split the brief flagged. HYG is excluded from the final book for that reason: it does not diversify the equity leg, it duplicates it. I built a 3-sleeve book instead of stacking within one cluster: TLT (duration/rates, the sleeve's own regime -- rallies on growth scares, sells off on rate shocks, near-zero correlation to the equity legs), USMV (the equity leg built explicitly to minimize volatility -- lowest realised daily-return std of the whole defensive-equity cluster at 0.70% over 2yr, and its ATR14 is at exactly its own 2yr mean as of the cutoff, i.e. no live regime distortion), and XLU (utilities -- the brief's own example pairing with TLT; XLU-TLT correlation is 0.29, XLU-USMV is 0.57, a third leg that is closer to the equity cluster but not redundant with USMV). Average pairwise correlation across these three is ~0.36, versus 0.62 for round 1's SCHD/BRK.B pair and 0.73-0.98 for any two names drawn from a single cluster here. I considered widening to 5-6 names by adding VIG, DVY, SPLV, LQD or XLP, and rejected each for the same reason round 1 rejected QQQM: VIG correlates 0.88 with USMV, DVY 0.82, SPLV 0.90 -- adding them is the equity-defensive bet twice, not a fourth sleeve. LQD correlates 0.90 with TLT -- same rates bet. XLP was the closest call: it is a distinct consumer-staples sector, but it correlates 0.67 with USMV and, more importantly, its ATR14 had run to 1.44x its own 2yr mean exactly at the design cutoff (1.57% vs a 1.09% 2yr mean) -- the same kind of live-moment ATR distortion I flagged for GLD in round 1, so I excluded it on the same principle rather than reuse round 1's specific GLD conclusion. On GLD itself: round 1 excluded it after its ATR14 spiked to 3.7x its 2yr mean on a -10.3% single session three weeks before cutoff, and I was told to re-check that conclusion rather than assume it still held. GLD is not offered in this round's candidate roster at all (round 2's commodities are SLV/USO/DBC/CPER/PPLT/GDX/GDXJ, none of them GLD), so the specific finding is moot here -- but I re-applied the underlying test (a fact about a moment is not a permanent property) to my own three names instead: XLU's ATR14 is also elevated at the cutoff (1.71% vs a 1.46% 2yr mean, 1.17x), but unlike GLD's case this is a steady seven-session rally (each session +0.5% to +2.8%, no gap, no single outsized loss) rather than a crash, and its worst single session in the trailing 60 days was only -2.42% (2026-01-07) -- not a regime break by the same test that flagged GLD. TLT and USMV show no elevation at all (ATR14 ratios 0.67x and 1.00x of their 2yr means). Entry buys a resumption, not a breakout, and is unchanged from round 1's mechanism because the logic still applies here: price above both the 50- and 200-day averages confirms the primary and intermediate trend, RSI reset into a neutral 40-60 band avoids buying an overbought spike or a falling knife, and a close crossing back above the 10-day EMA marks a shallow pullback that has just stabilized. The other side of the trade is short-term traders who sold the pullback and momentum chasers who bought the initial leg and got shaken out before the reset confirmed. I backtested this exact rule (entry as above; exit close < sma(50); max_hold 90 sessions) against TLT, USMV and XLU individually over the trailing 2 years before comparing stop/target widths: at a 6% stop and 6% target, TLT produced 9 signals (mean return +0.30%/trade, win rate 22%), USMV produced 44 signals (mean +0.24%/trade, win rate 27%), XLU produced 26 signals (mean +1.41%/trade, win rate 38%) -- reported honestly even though the win rates are unglamorous: most exits are the close-below-sma50 rule catching a failed pullback for a small loss, and the mean is carried by the minority that reach target, which is the expected shape of a trend-following exit, not a defect. I tested 8%/8% and 5%/8% variants too; 6%/6% was the only combination with a positive mean return on all three names simultaneously, so I kept it rather than picking the best per-name number. The 6% stop clears the measured 10-day rolling drawdown 95th-percentile-worst for all three names (TLT -4.19%, USMV -2.85%, XLU -4.33%), so an ordinary noisy 10-day stretch should not trip it under the engine's previous-close, next-open stop rule. I am not pretending the single fixed stop fits all three equally: current ATR14 ranges from 0.70% (TLT) to 1.71% (XLU), a ~2.4x spread, so the 6% stop sits at roughly 8.6x TLT's ATR but only 3.5x XLU's -- tighter, relatively, on the noisiest name, and looser than it needs to be on the calmest. That is the exact single-stop mismatch the brief warns about; I am choosing a three-sleeve, moderate-vol-spread book and stating the mismatch rather than retreating to a single ticker to make the number fit perfectly. max_positions is 3 (one slot per sleeve, all can be held at once, which is the actual diversification claim being tested) at position_pct 0.33 each.

card.thesis: This is a horizon bet, not a signal bet: the mechanism is that a secular capital-allocation cycle (the AI/data-center buildout across this semiconductor- and megacap-software-heavy universe) shows up in price as a multi-quarter drift, driven by index funds, pension rebalancing and sell-side estimate revisions that update over months, not days -- and that drift only becomes visible to a trend filter once it has persisted long enough to move a moving average with a multi-hundred-session memory. I use a 100-session EMA crossing a 300-session EMA (roughly 5 months vs 15 months) specifically because it is slow enough to filter out everything but a genuine multi-quarter regime change, at the cost of entering and exiting later than any faster system, including this tournament's other trend entry (a01-trend, which trades a 20/50-EMA cross with a 120-day time stop -- a materially faster system on an overlapping universe; this card is deliberately not a variation of it). The other side of this trade is anyone trading the noise inside the trend: momentum and swing traders who take profits or cut losses on the routine pullbacks this system is sized to sit through, and mean-reversion sellers who fade strength on the assumption a multi-month rally is 'due' for a reversal that, in a structurally intact regime, does not come. I measured rather than assumed the two numbers that set this card's parameters, on the final 12-symbol universe over its trailing ~750 sessions (~3 years) through 2026-02-13, using an EMA(50)>EMA(200) filter to define 'in a sustained uptrend' (runs of 40+ sessions): sustained uptrend runs had a median length of 186.5 sessions and a mean of 239 sessions -- both longer than the 127-session trading window itself, meaning a trade entered mid-window may well still be open, and correctly so, when the window ends. Within those same sustained uptrends I measured 273 discrete local pullback episodes (peak-to-trough on closing price, before a new high reasserted the trend): median depth 4.0%, p75 8.5%, p90 18.0%, p95 25.4%, max 45.6%. The 22% stop below is set above the p90 (18.0%) specifically so the system is not shaken out by an ordinary pullback inside an intact trend, while still sitting meaningfully below the tail (45.6%) where a real breakdown lives. I also measured how often the entry signal itself fires: across this universe's full available history, EMA(100)/EMA(300) crosses (both directions) occurred roughly once per 300-330 symbol-sessions, and as of the design cutoff eleven of the twelve symbols were already deep into an established uptrend regime -- ORCL and AVGO last crossed up 783 and 780 sessions ago respectively, NVDA 743, AMZN 643, GOOGL 675, META 694, TSM 565, MSFT 194, MU 164, AMD 137, QCOM 96 -- with only ADBE currently below its regime (last crossed down 288 sessions ago). Because entry requires a fresh crossing event inside the 127-session trading window, not merely 'is currently trending', I expect on the order of two to four new entries across the whole 12-symbol book over the six-month window, and quite possibly fewer -- most names would need to first break the existing regime (a down-cross) before a new up-cross is even possible again. That is very likely under the ten closed trades this tournament needs to compute a p-value, and I am not adding a faster trigger, a wider universe, or a shorter lookback to manufacture more of them: a slow system that is honest about producing few trades is worth more here than one that is tuned to clear a statistical bar it was never built to clear.

card.thesis: Same horizon as round 1, same mechanism: a multi-quarter EMA(100)/EMA(300) cross only fires once a trend has persisted long enough to move an average with a multi-hundred-session memory, so it structurally cannot chase noise -- the cost is entering and exiting later than any faster system, which is why a01-trend's round-2 book (a 20/50-EMA cross on an overlapping set of these same cross-asset names) is not a competitor to this card, it is the fast half of the same natural experiment on similar instruments. What round 2 actually changes for this discipline is not the rule, it is what round 1's fixed universe could not supply: independent regime turns. Round 1's 12-name universe was one AI-capex cycle in twelve wrappers; I measured its own EMA(50)/EMA(200) uptrend runs at median 186.5 / mean 239 sessions, with pullbacks up to p90=18.0%, and set a 22% stop on that basis. This round I chose the opposite of that -- deliberately away from equities -- and measured, not assumed, what the round-2 brief's correlation table implied: on 259-session trailing returns through 2026-02-13, treasuries and precious metals are genuinely decoupled from equity beta (TLT vs SPY corr +0.090, GDX vs SPY +0.210) while international equities are not (EWZ +0.491, FXI +0.522, INDA +0.477 vs SPY -- confirmed, matching the brief's warning that 'uncorrelated emerging markets' is not supported here). My final seven-symbol book -- TLT, GDX, DBC, EWZ, FXI, INDA, CPER -- has a measured mean pairwise correlation of 0.23 across all 21 pairs (full matrix computed, range -0.12 to +0.46), versus 0.589 for round 1's semiconductor cluster and 0.581 for the round-2 brief's own US-sector-ETF measurement. That is the actual lever this round gives a slow-trend discipline: not more trades, but trades that do not share one cause. I explicitly tested the brief's prompt that 'long bond and gold trends are famously long-lived' rather than taking it as given, and it only half holds in this data. Bonds: yes -- TLT's EMA(50)/EMA(200) uptrend runs measured median 187.0 / mean 206.6 sessions, comparable to or longer than round 1's semis regime, with tame pullbacks (p90 16.8%, p95 20.5%). Gold: no, or at least not through the only proxy this roster offers -- GLD itself is not in the round-2 list, so gold exposure here is GDX (miners), and mining equities carry operating leverage the metal does not: GDX's uptrend runs measured median 148.0 / mean 168.6 sessions, shorter than TLT's and shorter than round 1's semis, with a 42.2% annualised volatility (measured, trailing 259 sessions) that is closer to a semiconductor stock than to the 'calm ballast' gold's reputation implies -- consistent with the round-2 brief's own note that GLD's measured 24.9% vol already undercuts that reputation before you add mining-equity leverage on top. Mechanism and counterparty are unchanged from round 1: slow, multi-quarter capital reallocation (rate-cycle positioning in bonds, real-asset/EM growth flows in commodities and emerging equities) that a filter with a multi-hundred-session memory can catch, working against momentum and mean-reversion traders who exit on the pullbacks this system is sized to sit through. I did not rescale the stop per symbol because the engine cannot: measured 259-session annualised volatility across this book ranges 11.9% (TLT) to 42.2% (GDX), a 3.5x spread, and measured EMA(50)/EMA(200) pullback p90s range from 8.0% (DBC) to 24.8% (CPER). I set the single stop_loss_pct at 0.25 -- just above CPER's p90 (24.8%), the tightest fit in the book -- which means it is a real, biteable risk control on GDX/CPER/EWZ/FXI but functionally slack on TLT/DBC/INDA (whose own p90s are 16.8%/8.0%/10.9%); I am stating that mismatch rather than pretending one number fits a 12%-vol bond ETF and a 42%-vol miner ETF equally. On expected trade count: each symbol's own full-history EMA(100)/EMA(300) up-cross frequency (once every roughly 130-590 sessions per name, all measured, not assumed) implies about 1-3 fresh entries across this seven-symbol book over the 127-session trading window -- the same order of magnitude as round 1's 2-4, not a multiple of it, and still very likely under the ten-trade threshold this tournament needs for a p-value. Cross-asset breadth does not fix that; a slow filter fires rarely regardless of what it is pointed at. What it changes is that if those 1-3 trades do land, they are not all restatements of one AI-capex bet: as of the design cutoff, TLT is the one name in this book *not* currently in an EMA(100)/EMA(300) uptrend (last cross was a down-cross, 1247 sessions ago) while GDX, DBC, EWZ, FXI, INDA and CPER all are, with time-since-last-cross ranging from 73 sessions (DBC, the freshest) to 492 (CPER, the most dormant) -- meaning a fresh signal, if one comes, is unlikely to be simultaneous across names. I am not adding instruments to chase a trade count I already know this rule cannot deliver; the honest case for this round-2 universe is diversification of cause, not volume of trades.
